articles.title: IMF to Thailand: Shield Indebted Households, Not Fuel Prices, as ASEAN Peers Pull Ahead - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: IMF to Thailand: Shield Indebted Households, Not Fuel Prices, as ASEAN Peers Pull Ahead  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
As ASEAN peers ride the tech boom, IMF says Thailand's 2.1% growth leaves little cushion and urges targeted help for debt-laden households, not fuel caps.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged Thailand to support vulnerable, highly indebted households with targeted aid rather than broad energy subsidies, warning that the country’s fiscal buffers are shrinking while regional peers surge ahead on a technology boom.
The recommendation was delivered Thursday (October 15) during a press briefing on the Asia and Pacific economic outlook at the 2026 IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
Thailand is projected to grow just 2.1 per cent in both 2026 and 2027, according to the Fund's Regional Economic Outlook, released at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok.
That compares with 4.9 per cent for ASEAN as a whole this year, 8.4 per cent for Vietnam and 5.2 per cent for Malaysia. The 2026 figure was raised by 0.6 percentage points from April.
Asked how far household debt is holding back consumption, Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, said successive shocks – the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, tariffs and now the energy shock – had worn down fiscal buffers across the region.
"This is the time to embark upon growth-friendly fiscal consolidation that does not hurt those hit by the shocks," he said.
Governments should use social registries and digitalisation to deliver targeted support, anchored in a well-defined medium-term fiscal framework that reassures investors. The guiding principle, he said, is to "protect people and not prices".
The report details Thailand's own response to the oil shock, which began in February. Bangkok capped fuel prices with subsidies, released petroleum reserves, diversified procurement, restricted some exports, introduced work-from-home arrangements and offered cash transfers and cost-of-living top-ups.
Price-smoothing measures helped contain the pass-through of higher energy costs to inflation, the report said, but the baht came under depreciation pressure, as did the currencies of Indonesia, India and the Philippines, although this has partly eased.
The IMF warned that few such measures across the region are time-bound or clearly targeted and that exit strategies remain unclear in some economies. Broad fuel subsidies and price controls are costlier and weaken incentives to cut demand, it said.
The Fund also flagged longer-term concerns relevant to Thailand.
Its analysis of social safety nets said ageing economies such as Thailand must ensure households have decent incomes in retirement, and that policy should focus on making consumption more resilient among vulnerable, highly indebted households.
It also urged continued work on the "Bangkok Blueprint", the joint IMF, World Bank and Bank of Thailand framework against cyber-enabled financial fraud, which it called a rapidly emerging regional threat.
Growth in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is forecast at 4.9 per cent this year and 4.7 per cent in 2027, upgrades of 0.4 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, driven largely by technology-related exports and investment.
Vietnam leads at 8.4 per cent in 2026, up 1.3 points. Malaysia is projected at 5.2 per cent and Indonesia at 5.1 per cent. By contrast, the Philippines (3.4 per cent) and Cambodia (3.0 per cent) were cut by 0.7 and 1.0 points.
Srinivasan said ASEAN's energy intensity is about 7 per cent of GDP, higher than Asia's 4 per cent average, leaving some members especially vulnerable if the shock persists. Malaysia and Brunei, as energy exporters, are benefiting.
He urged Indonesia to keep subsidies targeted within its 3 per cent deficit anchor, which markets watch closely, and urged Malaysia to continue fiscal consolidation by broadening the tax base and trimming incentives and subsidies.
On artificial intelligence, he said ASEAN's priority should be skills and lifelong learning.
Asia's growth is projected to ease from 5.0 per cent in 2025 to 4.8 per cent in 2026 and 4.4 per cent in 2027, though 2026 is 0.4 points stronger than April's forecast.
The region will still contribute about two-thirds of global growth – 68 per cent, Srinivasan said.
The IMF credits three forces: adaptation to the oil shock through inventory drawdowns, alternative suppliers and renewables; an AI-driven boom in semiconductors and data centres; and trade that has held up better than feared, helped by surging intra-Asian commerce.
But "resilience is not unlimited", he said, noting that inventories cannot be drawn down indefinitely and fiscal costs are rising.
Risks are tilted to the downside: a prolonged or renewed Middle East escalation, a reassessment of AI profitability, fiscal strains and higher sovereign borrowing costs, and a potentially severe El Niño that could worsen food and energy inflation. Faster AI productivity gains or more predictable trade arrangements could provide upside.
China is forecast to grow 4.5 per cent this year and 4.0 per cent in 2027. Mr Srinivasan said domestic demand remains weak, rebalancing has not materialised and inflation is hovering near deflation.
He called for greater near-term fiscal stimulus and repeated the Fund's call for property-sector support worth about 5 per cent of GDP over three years, including triaging developers.
Korea's growth is forecast to accelerate to 3.3 per cent from 1.1 per cent in 2025, a 1.4-point upgrade. Japan is projected at 0.7 per cent.
Report figures show Korea's current account surplus reaching a record 19 per cent of GDP in 2026, against about 4 per cent for Japan, reflecting Korea's dominance in memory chips.
Sonali Jain-Chandra, the department's deputy director, warned that such concentration heightens vulnerability to any correction in AI demand but said Korea's tight monetary stance remains appropriate, with windfall tax revenues being saved.
India's growth is forecast at 7.0 per cent in 2026 and 2027, up 0.5 points, after a stronger-than-expected first quarter, with medium-term growth of 6.9 per cent.
Srinivasan said the rupee should not be treated as a gauge of economic success and called India's GDP data revisions consistent with good practice.
Bangladesh's growth was cut by 1.1 points to 3.6 per cent. Jain-Chandra said inflation hit 8 per cent in September, tight monetary policy must continue, and revenue, at about 7 per cent of GDP, is among the world's lowest. The IMF is in talks on a new programme requested in May.
On Sri Lanka, she said staff-level agreement on the seventh review was reached in early October, with another review before the programme expires in March. Any follow-on arrangement is the government's choice. She also stressed central bank independence in Nepal.
Pacific island economies are projected to grow 2.6 per cent this year, a 0.2-point downgrade, hit by food and fuel costs. Low-income economies also saw sizeable cuts.
The IMF's analysis of millions of online job postings found employer demand for AI-exposed jobs fell by as much as 10 per cent but has since stabilised, suggesting, Srinivasan said, that AI is "reshaping" the labour market rather than eliminating work.
The region needs nearly 150 million jobs over the next decade, the Fund's blog said.

articles.title: Singapore key exports jump by higher-than-expected 68.4% in September, led by non-electronics - The Business Times
articles.summary: Singapore key exports jump by higher-than-expected 68.4% in September, led by non-electronics  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
Electronics exports continue to surge on AI-related demand, but economists warn that this will soften in 2027
[SINGAPORE] The Republic’s non-oil domestic exports (NODX) surged 68.4 per cent year on year in September, more than double the 32.2 per cent consensus forecast of private-sector economists in a Bloomberg poll.
Driven by non-electronics NODX, the latest showing also extended August’s revised 46.1 per cent expansion, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) data showed on Friday (Oct 16).
This was the strongest print since February 1980, said OCBC chief economist Selena Ling.
Electronics exports growth remained robust, and watchers agreed that the trend should hold in the near term. But they noted that artificial intelligence-related tailwinds will begin to soften in 2027.
In the first nine months of 2026, NODX grew 27.6 per cent year on year.
Underpinned by this robust year-to-date growth, RHB upgraded its full-year NODX to 25 per cent, from 15.5 per cent.
Ling also observed upside risk to OCBC’s full-year forecast of 20 per cent, even if growth in the final quarter moderates to 11.5 per cent on year, considering base effects.
Non-electronics shipments expanded 54.2 per cent on the year in September, significantly higher than August’s 11.9 per cent, which EnterpriseSG primarily attributed to “the lumpy exports of structures of ships and boats”.
But it did not cite the year-on-year growth rate, “as the exceptionally high percentage growth reflects a low base effect in the same period last year”.
Other key drivers of the non-electronics NODX increase were non-monetary gold (124.3 per cent) and specialised machinery (50.4 per cent).
Meanwhile, electronics exports soared 107.6 per cent on a yearly basis in September, supported by robust AI-related demand. This was down from 131.6 per cent in the preceding month.
The growth was mainly led by disk media products (312.4 per cent), integrated circuits (74.7 per cent) and PCs (149.5 per cent).
Still growing
Electronics NODX grew 89.5 per cent year on year so far in 2026; and non-electronics, 8.2 per cent, Ling noted.
She said: “Despite recent equity market volatility in AI-related names, fundamentals such as earnings growth and order books, as well as domestic leading indicators such as the manufacturing and electronics Purchasing Managers’ Indexes, remain healthy.”
She thus believes that near-term export momentum should hold up, even as headline NODX growth moderates on higher base effects.
Said DBS senior economist Chua Han Teng: “Notably, electronics PMI sub-indices such as new export orders, and order backlogs have remained on an uptrend, while inventories are drawn down.”
RHB group chief economist Barnabas Gan and associate research analyst Laalitha Raveenthar expect that resilient AI demand and the ongoing tech upcycle should underpin export momentum through year-end.
While the three-month moving average growth of several key electronics products moderated in September, electronics exports remained robust, suggesting that underlying technology demand remains firm despite some moderation in product-level growth momentum, they said.
Global semiconductor sales, which reportedly reached a record US$159.7 billion in August 2026, also point to the broader semiconductor cycle remaining supportive, the pair added. “The global AI investment cycle is expected to remain a key growth support, even as AI-driven growth moderates from its exceptional pace.”
Eventual slowdown
Still, RHB’s duo flagged a quarter-on-quarter manufacturing output contraction in the third quarter, reversing from the second quarter’s expansion. While this does not necessarily signal a turning point, they said that the pullback warrants caution over the durability of growth in the coming quarters.
Economists cautioned that AI-led demand looks set to moderate in the longer term.
Ling pointed out: “The risk is that the current investment cycle begins to mature into 2027.”
Private-sector economists believe that AI-related spending will ease from the high levels in 2026, especially in the second half of next year, weakening demand for Singapore’s exports.
RHB said that MAS highlighted the possibility of an “AI infrastructure credit shock”, where weaker-than-expected AI monetisation could prompt hyperscalers to pare back capital expenditure, triggering a repricing of debt-financed AI investments.
“This could tighten financial conditions, delay projects along the AI supply chain and create a self-reinforcing downturn in investment and global growth,” the RHB duo added.
Standard Chartered’s chief economist Edward Lee and senior economist Jonathan Koh explained: “A sharper or more sustained correction in AI-related assets could pose an additional downside risk if tighter financing conditions cause technology firms to reassess AI capex.”
UOB associate economist Jester Koh added that higher global interest rates that could instill a degree of caution among firms about undertaking new investments.
Beyond technology-related risks, economists also named geopolitical tensions, crude oil price volatility, trade restrictions and a weaker US economy as key headwinds.
Breakdown by market
In September, key exports to Singapore’s top 10 markets – except India – rose. NODX to India fell 5.6 per cent, in a turnaround from the 23.6 per cent growth recorded in August.
UOB’s Koh said: “By destination, electronics NODX to markets deeply embedded in the semiconductor value chain remained robust.”
Key exports to the US rose 73.2 per cent year on year; the rise for Taiwan was 96.9 per cent, and for South Korea, 96 per cent.
Key exports to the EU grew 11.3 per cent in September, reversing from the 1.7 per cent fall in the previous month. In September, the EU was the only market out of Singapore’s top 10 to record a decline in NODX.

articles.title: Malaysia’s growth tops forecasts as AI boom drives export surge - The Business Times
articles.summary: Malaysia’s growth tops forecasts as AI boom drives export surge  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
GDP is up 5.3% in the three months to September from the year-ago period
[KUALA LUMPUR] Malaysia’s economic growth slowed but still exceeded expectations, as the artificial-intelligence boom continued to bolster exports and domestic demand remained resilient.
Gross domestic product rose 5.3 per cent in the three months to September from the year-ago period, going by advance estimates from the Department of Statistics Malaysia on Friday (Oct 16), beating the 5.1 per cent median prediction in a Bloomberg survey.
Third-quarter growth, however, slowed from the 6 per cent expansion in the previous three-month period.
Growth in Q3 was underpinned by positive performance in most economic sectors, the department said. Only the mining and quarrying sector contracted, it added.
The better-than-expected reading underscores the resilience of Malaysia’s economy, even as growth moderates from a strong first half.
Robust domestic consumption and demand for electronics used in AI have helped cushion the trade-dependent economy from disruptions caused by the US war against Iran.
“The out turn is broadly in line with our forecast and suggests the growth momentum remains robust, albeit moderating from strong growth in the first half of 2026,” said Lavanya Venkateswaran, economist at OCBC. “This very much leaves the door open for Bank Negara Malaysia to normalise its policy rate by 25 basis points. Our baseline for the adjustment is in January, but it is a close call for the November meeting.”
The ringgit was steady at 4.08 per US dollar after the GDP print, while local stocks held losses.
The services sector rose 5.4 per cent, bolstered by wholesale and retail trade, information and communication as well as finance, the statistics department said.
Manufacturing strengthened by 7.5 per cent, backed in part by export-oriented industries, particularly electrical and electronic products.
Bank Negara Malaysia governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said on Thursday that the economy is likely to grow about 5 per cent in 2026, with the nation’s diverse sources of growth helping cushion it against any slowdown in the AI boom.
The economy grew 5.5 per cent during the three quarters of 2026, the statistics department said, above the government’s revised growth forecast of 4.8 to 5.3 per cent for the year.
The government in October raised the forecast from 4 to 5 per cent previously.
Household spending remains firm, as fuel subsidies helped shield consumers from elevated energy cost. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim earlier in October also announced more cash aid and a higher minimum wage for next year to ease cost-of-living pressures.
The government expects the country’s economy to grow at a range of 4.2 to 5.2 per cent in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity.
Preliminary GDP data, which will provide a detailed analysis of Q3, will be released on Nov 18. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Myanmar’s military-backed government has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee in order to support its efforts to reintegrate itself into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The Southeast Asian bloc has excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since late 2021, due to its failure to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus plan. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.
The Irrawaddy reported yesterday that the new body, which met for the first time on Tuesday, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit next month, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the 11-nation organization. Tuesday’s meeting was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and attended by representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare.
Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” from ASEAN since 2021, The Irrawaddy reported. The meeting also discussed “Myanmar‑led approaches” for restoring the country’s position in the bloc.
Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government has launched a diplomatic charm offensive, involving visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.
A priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Many of the latter’s member states appear to be supportive of Naypyidaw’s goal, and five of them – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
The Philippines also appears to be softening. In a recent interview, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN for 2026, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.
At the same time as it has wooed individual ASEAN member states, the military-backed government has forcefully rejected the Five-Point Consensus. In July, Myanmar’s military proxy parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, which “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” Min Aung Hlaing said in a speech the following month that some member states had “adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar.”
While most member states are now leaning in the direction of reopening ASEAN’s door to Myanmar – Thailand and Malaysia have both explicitly stated that this is their goal, and Singapore and Timor-Leste appear to be the last hold-outs – full normalization, like all ASEAN decisions, will require a consensus among all 11 member states. As I noted earlier this week, however, there are “evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end.”
Unless ASEAN agrees to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether, normalization would seem to require at least some effort to implement it, however nominal. With the Myanmar military ramping up its attacks on resistance groups and civilian populations accused of harboring them, this seems unlikely in the current circumstances.

articles.title: Exports are growing strongly, creating momentum to achieve the 2026 target. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Exports are growing strongly, creating momentum to achieve the 2026 target.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Manufacturing of disposable sterile plastic products and medical supplies at Vietnam Medical Plastics Joint Stock Company, Tam Diep Industrial Park.
 Strong growth in key industries.
 Amidst the complex developments in the global economy and numerous adjustments to tariff policies in major markets, Ninh Binh's export activities have continued to achieve positive results. According to the socio-economic report of the Provincial People's Committee, export turnover in the third quarter is estimated at 10,622 million USD, an increase of 43.1%; the cumulative figure for the first nine months reached 28,132 million USD, an increase of 50% compared to the same period in 2015.
 According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade's assessment, this result is equivalent to 86.8% of the 2026 plan. Notably, export growth was recorded in many key product groups. Electronic components are estimated at US$11,256.6 million, an increase of 38.1%; computers and computer components reached US$2,854.5 million, an increase of 67.3%; garments reached US$3,156.7 million, an increase of 116.4%; footwear reached US$1,856.2 million, an increase of 30%; and automobiles and automobile components reached US$502.5 million, an increase of 30.8%.
 The province's export products are present in more than 100 countries and territories, with many large enterprises participating in global supply chains. This result is based on the development of industrial production. The industrial production index for the first nine months is estimated to have increased by 25.01%, with the processing and manufacturing industry increasing by 25.38%. Demand for electronic products, electrical equipment, and some consumer goods has improved, creating favorable conditions for businesses to maintain production and expand their scale. The structure of export products is also gradually becoming more diversified, with contributions from the electronics, computer, mechanical, and automotive industries alongside textiles and footwear.
 Comrade Nguyen Thanh Binh, Deputy Director of the Department of Industry and Trade, said: Following the direction of the Provincial Party Committee, the Provincial People's Council, and the Provincial People's Committee, the Department of Industry and Trade has implemented solutions to support businesses in developing markets and taking advantage of incentives from Free Trade Agreements (FTAs). Emphasis has been placed on disseminating commitments, rules of origin, and tax exemption and reduction schedules, helping businesses gain more information to organize production and choose suitable markets.
 Over the past nine months, the Department of Industry and Trade organized two conferences to disseminate knowledge, enhance the effectiveness of international economic integration, and publicize the Vietnam-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, with the participation of 300 delegates. Simultaneously, the Department issued nearly 10,000 certificates of origin (C/O) and approval documents according to its delegated authority. These activities directly support and facilitate businesses in meeting origin requirements, accessing tariff preferences, and boosting exports.
 Despite the high export turnover, the province's export activities still have limitations that need to be fully recognized. According to the Department of Industry and Trade's assessment, most of the province's large-scale export businesses operate as processing enterprises, dependent on foreign partners for both raw materials and consumer markets. Businesses have not yet proactively managed their value chains and distribution networks; intrinsic added value remains low compared to the scale of exports.
 This dependence makes production vulnerable to changes in orders, raw material prices, and trade policies. Meanwhile, textiles, footwear, agricultural products, and seafood continue to face competitive pressure from countries with similar production conditions. Major markets are increasingly focusing on technical standards, food safety, traceability, environmental protection, and sustainable development; some products also face the risk of trade defense investigations. In addition, fluctuations in international transportation and high shipping costs affect the price and competitiveness of goods.
 Supporting businesses in maintaining market share and expanding orders.
 At the 4th Session of the 16th Provincial People's Council on July 28, 2026, Resolution No. 52/NQ-HĐND was passed, adjusting and supplementing the growth targets for implementing Resolution No. 169/NQ-CP dated June 27, 2026 of the Government . Accordingly, the export turnover target for 2026 is a 23% increase compared to 2025. The results of the first nine months provide a favorable basis for achieving this target, but the tasks for the remaining months of the year still require proactive measures, especially in light of the unpredictable fluctuations in the international market.
 According to Mr. Nguyen Thanh Binh, Deputy Director of the Department of Industry and Trade, in the remaining months of the year, along with closely monitoring market developments, the Department of Industry and Trade will continue to support businesses in effectively exploiting traditional markets and seeking new markets; strengthening the provision of information on demand, technical standards, rules of origin, and trade policies in each market. Trade promotion and business networking activities need to focus on specific industries and markets; and at the same time, support businesses in better utilizing the benefits from FTAs.
 The Department of Industry and Trade has identified the need to strengthen coordination with specialized agencies of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Vietnamese trade offices abroad, and closely monitor policy adjustments in major economies such as the United States , China, the EU, and Japan. Timely updates on tariff regulations, trade barriers, and technical standards are directly relevant to industries that contribute significantly to the province's export turnover.
 Along with maintaining existing markets, the province's trade promotion activities will focus on supporting strong product lines such as electronic components, computers, automobiles and auto parts, textiles, footwear, handicrafts, and processed agricultural products; expanding markets to help businesses find more partners and reduce dependence on a few large markets; and applying information technology and digital transformation in trade promotion to expand customer reach and product promotion.
 To effectively utilize Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), the issuance of Certificates of Origin (C/O) needs to continue to be carried out smoothly and in accordance with regulations, coupled with guidance for businesses to meet origin requirements. Controlling and preventing origin fraud and illegal transshipment is essential to protect the reputation of goods and the rights of legitimate businesses. Tariff preferences are only effective when documentation is complete, the origin of raw materials is clearly stated, and compliance is ensured throughout the entire production process.
 The Provincial People's Committee also directed relevant departments to continue reviewing and gathering information, promptly resolving difficulties for industrial enterprises; ensuring safe and stable electricity supply for production. Programs for developing e-commerce and trade promotion are being implemented in conjunction with supporting technological innovation, improving product quality, expanding supply chains and import/export markets.
 For businesses, the immediate task is to maintain stable production, ensure quality, and meet delivery deadlines. In the long term, technological innovation, efficient use of raw materials, meeting environmental standards, and increasing linkages with domestic suppliers will contribute to increasing added value and consolidating their position in the production chain.
 The final months of the year are a time for Ninh Binh to accelerate its efforts to achieve its export targets and contribute to the province's overall growth. The support of management agencies, along with the proactive approach of businesses in each order and market, will help maintain the growth momentum and create a more solid foundation for export activities in the coming years.

articles.title: By attracting semiconductor investment, Vietnam is creating depth for its ecosystem. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: By attracting semiconductor investment, Vietnam is creating depth for its ecosystem.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to Vietnam's Semiconductor Industry Development Strategy with a vision to 2050, Vietnam aims to participate in all stages of the global semiconductor value chain, from design and manufacturing to packaging and testing.
The wave of investment in artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and electric vehicles is driving global chip demand, opening up opportunities for Vietnam to participate more deeply in the semiconductor industry.
However, to translate its investment-attracting advantages into genuine competitiveness, Vietnam needs to select appropriate market segments, develop a domestic supply chain, and address gaps in technology, human resources, capital, and infrastructure.
Opportunities from the global supply chain
According to the report “From AI to Electric Vehicles: How the APAC Semiconductor Industry Drives the Global Innovation Map” by FedEx, the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region accounts for approximately 58% of global semiconductor industry revenue.
The report indicates that Vietnam is benefiting from the trend of manufacturing relocation thanks to its electronics industry base, its position in the regional trade network, and its competitive labor force. Between 2006 and 2025, Vietnam's semiconductor exports are projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 31.8%, while imports are expected to increase by 30% annually. In 2023 alone, integrated circuit exports reached US$32.4 billion.
According to Ee-Hui Tan, Managing Director of FedEx Vietnam and Cambodia, Vietnam is becoming an increasingly important link in the APAC semiconductor ecosystem as many semiconductor and high-tech companies expand their operations there.
According to information from the Ministry of Science and Technology at the end of 2025, Vietnam had approximately 170 foreign direct investment (FDI) projects in the semiconductor sector, with a total registered capital of nearly US$11.6 billion.
The presence of Samsung , Intel, MediaTek, and many other technology corporations facilitates Vietnam's access to international technology, manufacturing processes, and customer networks. Furthermore, the electronics and components market is projected to reach $145 billion by the end of 2026, expanding the development potential for related industries.
However, the increase in investment and exports does not necessarily mean that Vietnam has mastered the high value-added stages in the semiconductor supply chain. The spillover effect of FDI depends on the level of participation of domestic enterprises in the supply chain, their capacity to adopt technology, and their ability to develop high-tech products and services. Without these linkages, production and exports may continue to increase while domestic technological capabilities remain limited.
This situation was mentioned by Mr. Thomas Pang, Acting CEO of Neuron Digital Group, at the Vietnam Innovation Summit 2026 (VIS 2026), organized by the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Science and Technology in collaboration with InnoLab Asia in Ho Chi Minh City recently.
According to Thomas Pang, semiconductor operations in Vietnam currently focus primarily on design, packaging, and testing. Upstream processes such as raw material and equipment supply and wafer fabrication are limited, while advanced downstream applications and system integration are still developing.

In fact, this is not a new story. Many experts have also pointed out that Vietnam needs to clearly identify the stages with potential for development based on existing capabilities, while simultaneously building a suitable upgrading roadmap. Expanding participation in the value chain must go hand in hand with the ability to accumulate technology, production experience, and form domestic supply chain links.
Choose the right market segment and develop the necessary foundational conditions simultaneously.
According to Vietnam's Semiconductor Industry Development Strategy to 2030, with a vision to 2050, Vietnam aims to participate in all stages of the global semiconductor value chain, from design and manufacturing to packaging and testing. However, to realize this goal, determining priorities and allocating resources appropriately is crucial.
Mr. Thomas Pang, Acting CEO of Neuron Digital Group, believes that to upgrade its position in the semiconductor value chain, Vietnam needs to clearly identify priority segments, leverage existing advantages, and focus on developing specialized capabilities instead of spreading resources too thinly. Besides its strengths in packaging and testing, shifting to higher value-added stages requires a consistent industrial development strategy and a synchronized coordination mechanism among regulatory agencies.
Since investment decisions in the semiconductor industry often have a 5-10 year timeframe, a stable, predictable policy environment and effective coordination mechanisms among regulatory agencies are necessary. According to Thomas Pang, the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) model, acting as a central hub for connecting and coordinating the activities of many relevant agencies, is an experience that Vietnam can learn from.
Besides policies and coordination mechanisms, digital infrastructure is also a crucial condition for enhancing the competitiveness of the semiconductor industry. Advanced manufacturing facilities generate large amounts of data on energy, environment, equipment, and logistics. The ability to integrate, analyze, and exploit this data to support decision-making will become increasingly significant for operational efficiency.
Among these, AI requires the right data to be effective, while digital twin technology and real-time data can support simulation, monitoring, and optimization of production operations and energy efficiency. Combining physical and digital infrastructure will contribute to improved investment efficiency and reduced operating costs, especially since advanced production facilities require significant initial capital.
“Vietnam has advantages in terms of geographical location, political stability, a young workforce, and the attention of policymakers. What Vietnam needs now is depth in its ecosystem. That depth must be built through a consistent strategy, coordinated efforts among agencies, and a smart infrastructure,” Thomas Pang emphasized.
Calvin Yong, Regional Director for Southeast Asia, India, and Oceania at Yole Group, believes that Vietnam needs to focus on addressing gaps in domestic supply chain capacity, manufacturing capabilities, and production management experience.
According to Calvin Yong, after about 25 years working in the semiconductor industry, he has observed that the majority of suppliers serving the industry in Vietnam are still foreign companies, while many inputs depend on imports. This highlights the need to develop a domestic supply network, helping Vietnamese businesses gradually participate more deeply in the production chains of international corporations.
To achieve this goal, large enterprises, small and medium-sized enterprises, and regulatory agencies need to coordinate efforts to improve production capacity, product quality, and the ability to meet stringent industry standards. Simultaneously, conditions should be created to allow domestic suppliers to participate in the networks of semiconductor corporations, thereby accumulating experience, enhancing technological capabilities, and expanding their operations.
Another gap lies in manufacturing capabilities, which play a crucial role in connecting the design process with commercial production. Vietnam already has a foundation in integrated circuit design engineering and technology development, but to move products from design to commercialization, it needs access to appropriate manufacturing capabilities.

Expanding from back-end processes like packaging and testing to front-end processes like semiconductor manufacturing can help complete the ecosystem. However, manufacturing requires significant capital investment, specialized technology, experienced personnel, and specific factory operating conditions. Therefore, investment decisions should be carefully considered based on market demand, actual capacity, and the potential for forming a supply chain, rather than simply expanding presence in existing processes.
Besides technology and supply capacity, production management experience is also a crucial factor. According to Calvin Yong, the Vietnamese semiconductor industry still needs personnel with direct experience in managing and operating factories, overseeing production, and implementing advanced packaging technology.
These are skills that are difficult to develop through theoretical training alone and must be accumulated through practical experience. Therefore, in addition to training engineers, attracting experienced experts, strengthening cooperation with international businesses, and creating opportunities for Vietnamese personnel to participate directly in production projects will contribute to shortening the process of accumulating these skills.
Amidst the ongoing restructuring of the global semiconductor supply chain, experts believe that Vietnam's opportunities lie not only in its ability to attract new projects but also in leveraging this process to accumulate knowledge, technology, and management experience.
Choosing the right direction and aligning development goals with available resources will determine the ability to shift to more technically demanding processes, thereby increasing the value created domestically.

articles.summary: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz  CNBCUpdate: Singapore confirms container ship sunk in Hormuz amid fresh Iran attacks  Seatrade Maritime NewsTwo Singapore-registered vessels struck in Strait of Hormuz; one sinks  ReutersShip attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow  BBCInternational Seaways grabs Bruton VLCC fleet in $370m merger deal  TradeWinds News
articles.full_text:
Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and lucrative shipping opportunities keep some operators willing to brave escalating attacks, maritime experts said.
The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away.
Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats.
"I don't see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity," Koh told CNBC.
His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe.
Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents.
Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran's continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation.
Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs.
Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages.
Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said.
Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers.
Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called "Hormuz shuttle" involving about 20 very large crude carriers.
The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official's account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks.
"Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the 'Hormuz shuttle,'" Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying.
Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said.
However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies' assessments of the risks, he added.
The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions.
"Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy," said association president TS Teo.
Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added.
While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait.
Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels.
That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said.
However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman's Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries.
"If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them," Krishna said.

The Deputy Prime Minister requested strengthened price management, ensuring the supply of essential goods, and strictly dealing with acts of speculation and hoarding in order to control inflation by the end of 2026.
The Government Office has just issued Notice No. 528/TB-VPCP dated October 15, 2026, summarizing the conclusions of Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang , Head of the Steering Committee for Price Management, at the meeting of the Steering Committee for Price Management regarding the results of price management and control in the third quarter and the first nine months of 2026; and the orientation for price management in the remaining three months of 2026.
The concluding statement indicated that, in the last three months of 2026, the unfavorable and unpredictable global economic situation, facing numerous risk factors, would continue to impact the domestic market and put pressure on inflation control efforts.
Against this backdrop, from now until the end of the year, the Deputy Prime Minister requested that ministries, sectors, and localities continue to coordinate closely, proactively, flexibly, synchronously, and effectively in managing fiscal, monetary, and other macroeconomic policies to control inflation, stabilize the macroeconomy, ensure major economic balances, and create room to support growth and enhance the economy's resilience to external shocks; at the same time, they need to continue to proactively monitor domestic and international economic developments, and promptly, decisively, and effectively implement tasks and solutions.
Strictly punish acts of speculation, hoarding, and price manipulation.
In this regard, the Deputy Prime Minister requested ministries, agencies, and localities to manage the prices of goods and services set by the State according to a suitable roadmap, carefully assess the impact on the CPI index, and ensure a balance between the goals of implementing the market-based roadmap, controlling inflation, and supporting the recovery of production and business.
Strengthen inspection and supervision of price declarations and listings for monitored sectors and fields, especially for essential goods; strictly handle acts of speculation, hoarding, and price manipulation aimed at illegal profiteering, and the exploitation of natural disasters, storms, floods, and peak holiday seasons to arbitrarily raise selling prices. Require businesses to promptly reduce selling prices accordingly when input material costs decrease to protect consumer rights. Direct the strict implementation of regulations on public disclosure of income and expenditure at the beginning of the school year, preventing the 발생 of any income outside the prescribed list.
Simultaneously, strengthen communication and provide timely and transparent information on the government 's price management policies and price fluctuations of essential goods. This will guide public opinion, stabilize consumer and business sentiment, and control inflation expectations. Strengthen the dissemination and training on new pricing regulations; proactively and urgently implement the process of receiving price declarations to promptly collect data for market aggregation, analysis, and forecasting.

Focus capital on production, business, and priority sectors.
The State Bank of Vietnam proactively and flexibly manages monetary policy, coordinating closely with fiscal policy; closely monitors developments in exchange rates, interest rates, credit, money supply, and international capital flows to proactively implement solutions to mitigate the impact of imported inflation; regulates credit growth appropriately, prioritizing capital allocation for production, business, and priority sectors.
The Ministry of Finance continues to effectively implement appropriate policies on tax, fee, and levy exemptions, reductions, and extensions to reduce input costs for businesses and support people's lives; advises and submits to the Prime Minister for consideration and issuance of a Prime Minister's directive on management, operation, and price stabilization in the remaining months of the year; and studies and reports to competent authorities on assigning targets for controlling the consumer price index to localities from 2027.
Ensure a balance between supply and demand for strategic commodities under all circumstances.
The Deputy Prime Minister requested the Ministry of Industry and Trade to closely monitor the price fluctuations of gasoline, liquefied petroleum gas, coal, electricity, and other energy sources in the domestic and international markets. The Ministry should manage domestic gasoline prices according to regulations, closely following global price trends and ensuring a balance between inflation control, macroeconomic stability, and maintaining supply. The Ministry should direct key enterprises to ensure the supply of gasoline for production, business, and consumption; preventing supply disruptions or hoarding in anticipation of price increases.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade shall preside over and coordinate with relevant ministries and agencies to regulate the supply and demand of essential goods nationwide, ensuring a balance between supply and demand for strategic commodities in all situations. It shall strengthen inspection and supervision of price declarations and price listings for goods under its management.
The Ministry of Agriculture and Environment closely monitors the production, supply, demand, and prices of essential food items. It proactively develops plans to ensure food supply in all situations, preventing localized shortages that could cause unusual price fluctuations. It strengthens disease prevention and control efforts for crops and livestock; promotes restocking and expansion of production for items at risk of supply shortages. It monitors and manages the prices of animal feed, fertilizers, and agricultural supplies; and proactively advises on solutions to stabilize supply and prices.
Actively coordinate with the Ministry of Industry and Trade and local authorities to regulate supply between regions, and appropriately balance domestic consumption and export demand for strategic agricultural products.
Develop a suitable roadmap for adjusting healthcare service prices.

The Ministry of Health closely monitors the prices of medicines, medical supplies, laboratory chemicals, medical equipment, and medical examination and treatment services; ensuring an adequate supply of medicines and medical supplies to meet the healthcare needs of the people at reasonable prices. It will develop a roadmap for adjusting medical service prices to suit people's affordability and contribute to inflation control. It will strengthen inspections of price declarations and price listings for medicines and medical supplies; and strictly handle violations of pricing laws.
The Ministry of Construction is responsible for monitoring and evaluating the price fluctuations of construction materials, housing, real estate, and construction costs; and proactively proposing solutions to stabilize the market. It directs localities to promptly update and publish construction material prices and construction price indices that closely reflect market developments; and to promptly address speculation, hoarding, or price manipulation of construction materials.
Coordinate with relevant agencies to strengthen inspections of declared and posted transportation fares. Require transportation businesses to adjust fares downwards accordingly when fuel costs decrease; strictly handle cases of delayed adjustments or those exploiting fluctuations in fuel prices to unreasonably increase fares.
The People's Committees of provinces and cities direct relevant agencies to closely monitor the supply and demand and prices of essential goods; proactively implement market stabilization programs and plans to ensure the supply of goods during the rainy season, storms, natural disasters, emergencies, and to meet the production and consumption needs at the end of the year.
For localities with CPI increases higher than the national average, the People's Committees of provinces and cities shall direct the Department of Finance to take the lead, in coordination with the Statistics agency and other relevant agencies, in conducting in-depth analysis and assessment of the factors forming prices and the causes of price fluctuations of commodity groups with high price increases; based on the authority of state management of prices at the local level, promptly implement effective and appropriate measures to manage and control key prices in line with market developments and the socio-economic situation in the locality to ensure price stability, contribute to controlling inflation, support macroeconomic stability and socio-economic growth and development.

articles.title: Beijing uses the South China Sea to corner Taiwan - GIS Reports
articles.summary: Beijing uses the South China Sea to corner Taiwan  GIS Reports
articles.full_text:
Maritime boundary disputes mask a bigger contest over Taiwan’s future.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
- Beijing sees disputes as leverage, not territorial strife
- Manila is firm on border policy while pragmatic in economics with Beijing
- Japan’s growing security role could fill gaps from American downsizing
Behind China’s opposition to the Japan-Philippines negotiations on maritime borders lies its desire to expedite a resolution to the Taiwan question by fueling territorial disputes in the South China Sea.
Based on the so-called nine-dash line principle, Beijing claims sovereignty over approximately 90 percent of the resource-rich South China Sea, an area that overlaps with the exclusive economic zones (EEZs) of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam.
On July 12, 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, Netherlands, found that China’s historical claims to the nine-dash line in the South China Sea lacked legal basis. However, the weight of this decision depends on the voluntary compliance and enforcement of the parties involved. The Chinese government has declared the arbitration worthless and maintains that the ruling disregards its historical rights in the sea. This has led to ongoing tension between China and affected countries, particularly the Philippines.
In late May 2026, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced that Japan and the Philippines had agreed to launch formal delimitation negotiations to set the limits of their overlapping exclusive economic zones and continental shelves in the waters east of Taiwan. Both sides hope to conclude these negotiations this year.
EEZs, territorial waters and continental shelves
In 1982, United Nations member states agreed to the Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), defining the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities, replacing the “freedom of the seas” concept from the 17th century. UNCLOS defines EEZs, territorial waters and continental shelves. China, Japan and the Philippines are signatories to the convention and have ratified it in their legislatures.
Territorial waters or seas give a nation full sovereignty – including control of navigation – over the waters out 12 nautical miles (22 kilometers) from its shores.
Exclusive economic zones stretch out a further 200 nautical miles (370 kilometers) from the edge of the territorial zone. A state has exclusive rights regarding the exploration and use of underwater and marine resources of the area, though in navigation terms, this part of the sea is itself considered international water.
A country’s continental shelf covers the seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas extending a minimum of 200 nautical miles (370 kilometers) from its coast, though it can be larger in some situations. Coastal nations have exclusive rights to explore and exploit the natural resources of their continental shelf, but do not own the territory.
The distance between Japan’s southwestern islands and the northernmost islands of the Philippines is less than 400 nautical miles, which naturally leads to overlapping claims regarding EEZs in waters east of Taiwan. Both countries hope to establish clear and peaceful boundaries in accordance with international law to clearly regulate maritime activities such as fishing and resource management while avoiding ambiguities. The delimitation negotiations are part of a broader effort to enhance bilateral trust, intelligence sharing and maritime security in the Indo-Pacific region. It is also designed as a move against China’s claims of the maritime territories in the respective region.
Beijing strongly protests these negotiations, claiming that the bilateral consultation process is illegal and the area in question infringes upon China’s asserted maritime rights. However, under UNCLOS Articles 74 and 83, adjacent coastal states have the right to resolve overlapping boundary issues through bilateral negotiations. If this model of bilateral negotiation and territorial demarcation takes hold, any two countries could team up to carve up the sea, specifically, areas claimed by a third country such as China. Nevertheless, Taiwan will be de facto “sandwiched” through the Tokyo-Manila negotiations.
China’s primary concern is not the specific territorial disputes in the South China Sea; rather, it is using this issue to expedite a resolution to the Taiwan question.
The Philippines’ strategy: Strong on territory, flexible with economics
Since many Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states are located around the South China Sea and have made sovereignty claims that differ from China’s, the intergovernmental forum has been working since 2013 to negotiate with China a rules-based Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, aimed at easing tensions and preventing conflicts. Yet due to China’s obstruction and to internal disagreements within ASEAN itself, these negotiations have yet to be concluded.
The Philippines and Vietnam are among the countries most actively promoting the protection of their territorial waters and EEZs. Other claimants, however, are adopting approaches that avoid offending China’s interests. For example, Malaysia recently has supported the One China principle and hinted that it might support China’s use of force to seize Taiwan. Meanwhile, Indonesia, despite having overlapping maritime sovereignty claims with China, conducted joint military exercises with China in August of this year in the sensitive waters east of Taiwan. In this regard, the Japan-Philippines negotiations are a reaction to ASEAN’s inaction in the face of escalating tensions between the South China Sea claimant states and China.
Disputed territories
China and the Philippines have already clashed in the South China Sea. The most recent incident occurred on July 24, 2026, when a Philippine government vessel entered the waters around Scarborough Shoal, a coral atoll in the disputed South China Sea waters. There have been more violent standoffs as well. In 2024, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said in his State of the Nation Address that the country “will not bow to bullies.”
To this end, the Philippines has decided to strengthen its military capabilities. Given the vast disparity in military strength with China, Manila has opted for asymmetric warfare, actively developing drones and missile patrol vessels to enhance its strike and surveillance capabilities. It has also joined forces with other countries to uphold UNCLOS. The Philippines, Japan and the United States recently completed a round of joint defense exercises in the South China Sea. Meanwhile, the U.S.-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty provides a potential foundation for collective deterrence.
At the same time, Manila is strengthening its economic cooperation with both Washington and Tokyo. The Philippines has formally joined the Silicon Prosperity Initiative, a hub that serves as the backbone of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a multinational infrastructure and investment initiative linking Subic Bay, Clark, metro Manila and Batangas in the Philippines. The development program is promoted by Washington, Manila and Tokyo. The U.S. will provide $100 million in aid for its construction.
However, despite Manila’s tensions with China and its hard line against Beijing on territorial issues, the Marcos administration has also demonstrated diplomatic pragmatism and is cautiously cooperating with China in other areas. This approach appears to align with China’s short-term strategy.
President Marcos has publicly stated that he remains optimistic about economic relations between the two countries, with the war in Iran being a catalyst with a direct negative impact on the Philippines’ energy and fertilizer supplies. On March 17, the Philippines requested that China not interrupt fertilizer supplies. Chinese leaders agreed, ensuring the country’s needs for spring planting were met. The Philippines was also able to procure diesel fuel from China. President Marcos publicly thanked Beijing for its assistance. Currently, China and the Philippines are negotiating joint energy exploration efforts.
Japan’s role is growing
Although Japan is not a claimant in the South China Sea, it is a stakeholder in the rules-based order in the First Island Chain, the strategic geographic line of Pacific archipelagos including Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines. In July of this year, Japan and 13 other countries issued a joint statement marking the 10th anniversary of the international arbitration tribunal’s rejection of Beijing’s broad sovereignty claims over disputed areas in the South China Sea. Under the framework of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, the leaders of Japan and the Philippines agreed to launch negotiations on the General Security of Military Information Agreement as a first step toward future intelligence sharing and to explore the possibility of Japan transferring a warship to the Philippines.
This move by Japan is directly linked to Tokyo’s decision to shift its military from a postwar role of exclusive defense to a new presence capable of proactive deterrence and transnational intervention. This development also directly aligns with U.S. President Donald Trump’s gradual scaling back of the U.S. military presence in Asia and elsewhere, while simultaneously demanding that its traditional East Asian allies, like those in Europe, increase their defense spending. For varying reasons, countries like Indonesia and Vietnam welcome Japan’s expanding military, economic and diplomatic influence as a strategic third option.
The U.S. approach: Strengthen and stabilize regional states

articles.title: "Annual limit of 350,000 units" China concedes hybrid vehicle exports under EU trade pressure; prospects of difficulties in securing alternative markets and local production - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: "Annual limit of 350,000 units" China concedes hybrid vehicle exports under EU trade pressure; prospects of difficulties in securing alternative markets and local production  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Discussion expected on China trade imbalance and industry damage response at EU summit
China maintains optimism despite hybrid vehicle export limits, but market skepticism persists
Expansion of local production by Chinese automakers in Europe faces burdens from production costs and local procurement regulations
There are forecasts that trade relations with China will emerge as a key agenda at the European Union (EU) summit. As trade imbalances deepen and conflicts between the two sides intensify, international attention is focused on the EU’s further response measures. Recently, China has made some concessions, such as agreeing to limit hybrid vehicle export volumes amid tense trade relations, but considering sluggish domestic demand and high entry barriers in alternative export markets, it appears difficult to reduce dependence on Europe in the short term.
EU struggles with trade deficit against China
According to Reuters on the 14th (local time), leaders of the 27 EU member states will hold a summit on the 15th-16th in Brussels, Belgium, to discuss damage to regional industries and trade response measures caused by a surge in imports of Chinese automobiles and manufactured goods. The EU's trade deficit in goods with China reached 360 billion euros (about US$419 billion) last year, and hit 200 billion euros (about US$233 billion) in the first half of this year. This deficit is occurring not only in automobiles, which have been the main source of conflict between the two sides, but also across manufactured goods including machinery, textiles, basic metals, and chemicals, raising growing concerns over weakening competitiveness and employment declines among regional companies.
Meanwhile, the policy direction of the EU Commission is shifting toward curbing the influx of Chinese products into the region. A representative example is the imposition of high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Since 2023, the Commission has conducted an anti-subsidy investigation on Chinese EVs for about a year, and in July 2024, it imposed provisional countervailing duties on Chinese EVs, judging that Chinese government subsidies distorted competition in the regional market. This was the first large-scale trade sanction against Chinese EVs. In October of the same year, the EU finalized, with member states' approval, additional tariffs up to 35.3% on Chinese EVs per company. These tariffs are added to the existing 10% tariff on vehicle imports and will be applied from October 30, 2024, for five years.
China limits hybrid vehicle import volumes
Amid this trade pressure, China recently made some concessions in negotiations with the EU, easing tensions. On the 12th, the Financial Times reported that the Commission is pushing a plan to limit annual import volumes of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to 350,000 units. This agreement was reached during trade talks between Maroš Šefčovič, EU Commissioner for Trade, and Wang Wentao, China's Minister of Commerce, held in Beijing on the 8th-9th. The import limit will be implemented in December this year, setting an annual import cap at 350,000 units in 2027, with a 6% annual increase starting in 2028, through 2030.
The restriction applies to hybrid vehicles produced in China and exported to the EU, including vehicles manufactured by European automakers in their Chinese plants. However, vehicles of Chinese brands produced within the EU are exempt from the import quota. The EU estimates China's hybrid vehicle exports to the EU will reach about 800,000 units this year. This agreement aims to reduce the import volume of Chinese hybrid vehicles by more than half and lower their market share from the current approximately 6% to around 3% within the regional market.
"Exports will rather expand," China's confidence
On the other hand, China claims that this agreement creates opportunities for expanding exports of its enterprises. On the 12th, China's Ministry of Commerce released an official statement noting, "According to EU statistics, EU imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles were 107,000 units in 2024 and rose to 302,000 units in 2025," adding that "both sides agreed to expand imports based on 2025 volumes, ensuring export capacity and stable growth for Chinese companies." While the EU emphasizes the reduction effect based on expected imports this year, China highlights that the agreement allows increasing export volumes based on last year's actual import figure of 302,000 units.
Additionally, China’s Ministry of Commerce explained that the hybrid vehicle trade agreement is based on three principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination, and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Regarding the non-discrimination principle, it stated, "No measures should target only Chinese products or discriminate against Chinese companies," and added, "The import quota allocated to China will not be less than that allocated to any other import source country in the EU." On WTO compliance, it affirmed, "China retains all rights within the WTO framework, including initiating dispute settlement procedures and requesting trade remedies."
Table 1. Chinese Hybrid Vehicle Import Restriction Plan and Positions of Both Sides
| Category | Main content | 
|---|---|
| Import Restriction Plan | Set an annual import limit of 350,000 Chinese hybrid vehicles in 2027, with a 6% annual increase from 2028 through 2030 | 
| EU Position | Measure to reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle inflow by more than half compared to this year's expected imports and lower market share | 
| China's Position | Quota increases compared to last year's actual imports, making the agreement favorable for export expansion and stable growth | 
Difficulty in seeking alternative markets
However, skepticism remains about China's optimism in the market. There are concerns that China will face difficulties absorbing its existing European export volumes in other markets. First, the Chinese domestic automobile market is sluggish due to weakened consumer sentiment and reduced purchase subsidies. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), domestic passenger car sales in China were about 1.63 million units in September, a 28.1% year-on-year decline, marking the 12th consecutive month of decrease. Entry barriers in alternative export markets are also rising. The U.S. has imposed a 100% additional tariff on Chinese EVs and tightened regulations on Chinese connected car software and hardware, effectively blocking market entry. Mexico approved a bill last December imposing tariffs up to 50% on about 1,400 items, including automobiles imported from non-FTA countries such as China, while Brazil raised tariffs on imported electric and hybrid vehicles to 35% starting July.
Absorption capacity in existing major export markets is also limited. According to a March report by global accounting firm PwC, Chinese exports of passenger and light commercial vehicles to Russia fell sharply by 46% to about 556,000 units last year due to factors such as increased import taxes by the Russian government and weakening domestic vehicle demand. Southeast Asia, targeted by China as a new export hub, is relatively small in scale. PwC data shows that automobile sales in six major ASEAN countries—Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Philippines, Vietnam, and Singapore—totaled about 3.5 million units last year, with Chinese automakers holding only 11% market share.
Uncertain effectiveness of local production strategies
Under these circumstances, Chinese companies are striving to establish local production and supply chains in Europe to open new paths. On the 12th, Stella Li, BYD’s Senior Vice Chairman, told French economic broadcaster BFM Business in an interview that the company plans to secure two additional production hubs in Europe, with France being a strong candidate. BYD already built its first complete car production plant in Europe in Hungary, which is scheduled to begin full operation in the fourth quarter this year. Additionally, XPeng continues contract manufacturing through Magna International’s factory in Austria and is considering partnering with local manufacturers to build new factories or utilize existing ones. Changan Automobile also aims to expand its European production capacity to 180,000 units annually by 2028 and 350,000 units by 2030.
The problem is that expanding local production in Europe may not directly enhance the competitiveness of Chinese companies. They have to bear higher labor and energy costs in Europe compared to China and incur additional expenses while establishing new local parts supply chains. Furthermore, the direction of the EU’s industrial regulations remains unsettled. The Commission is currently promoting stricter local production and parts procurement requirements for EVs under the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), with ongoing debates among member states and industries over the scope of products recognized as European. Controversies persist over whether vehicles and parts produced in non-EU countries such as Turkey, the UK, and Morocco should be recognized as European. Chinese automakers risk additional burdens of adjusting their parts procurement and production systems depending on the regulations finalized in the future.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's third-quarter 2026 advance gross domestic product (GDP) estimate of 5.3 per cent is a positive surprise despite external shocks, particularly the ongoing US-Iran conflict, economists said.
They told Business Times that while growth moderated from six per cent in the preceding quarter, the slowdown did not necessarily signal a broad-based loss of economic momentum.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said proactive government measures, including targeted fuel subsidies through MyKad introduced last year, had helped cushion the economy against external shocks.
Petroliam Nasional Bhd's efforts to secure fuel supplies from outside the Strait of Hormuz also helped minimise disruptions to domestic economic activity, he added.
Foreign investor interest in Malaysia and stronger demand for technology-related sectors had also supported growth, while full employment and relatively contained inflation helped sustain consumer spending.
"Overall, it is a positive surprise and it looks like the growth numbers could be surprised on the upside with the prevailing GDP growth projection currently standing between 4.8 per cent to 5.3 per cent," the economist said.
He added that growth of 5.3 per cent would put Malaysia's economy above its estimated trend growth rate of around 4.7 per cent.
According to the advance estimate released by the Statistics Department today, Malaysia's GDP is estimated to have grown 5.3 per cent in Q3, slightly higher than the 5.2 per cent recorded in the corresponding period last year.
Bank Negara Malaysia is scheduled to release the official Q3 GDP figures on Nov 18.
Growth eased from six per cent in the preceding quarter, with all economic sectors expanding except mining and quarrying.
For the first nine months of 2026, the economy grew 5.5 per cent, compared with 4.8 per cent in the same period last year.
The services sector remained the main growth driver, expanding 5.4 per cent, supported by wholesale and retail trade, information and communication, as well as finance and insurance activities.
Manufacturing growth accelerated to 7.5 per cent from 7.3 per cent in the preceding quarter, driven by export-oriented industries, particularly electrical, electronic and optical products, as well as petroleum, chemicals, rubber and plastics products.
Construction growth eased to six per cent from 6.5 per cent, supported by non-residential projects, particularly data centres, and specialised construction works.
The agriculture sector rebounded 1.3 per cent after contracting 3.7 per cent in the preceding quarter, driven by oil palm and livestock activities.
In contrast, mining and quarrying contracted 4.9 per cent, reversing the 9.2 per cent expansion recorded in the second quarter, following a decline in crude oil and condensate production.
Despite the expansion, Universiti Teknologi Mara senior lecturer Dr Mohamad Idham Md Razak said Malaysia should remain mindful of risks stemming from its exposure to global trade and the current AI investment cycle.
He said softer global technology spending could weigh on semiconductor exports, manufacturing activity and data centre investments.
Higher oil prices could raise businesses' operating costs and further erode household purchasing power.
"Another concern is whether domestic consumption can remain strong if wages fail to keep pace with living costs.
"Malaysia should therefore strengthen domestic economic resilience by improving productivity, supporting small and medium enterprises, attracting higher-value investments and developing new export markets.
"The priority is not simply to maintain headline growth, but to ensure that growth is broad-based and sustainable, so the economy can withstand external shocks without placing excessive pressure on households or public finances," Idham said.
He said Malaysia remains on a relatively solid growth trajectory, but sustaining this momentum will depend on domestic demand, the quality of investments and efforts to diversify the economy's growth drivers.

Export activities continued to record positive results. Merchandise export turnover in the first nine months reached US$434.30 billion, an increase of 24.5% compared to the same period last year, exceeding the target growth rate of 15-16% set for the whole year. In September alone, the merchandise trade balance recorded a surplus of US$1.27 billion, although the overall trade deficit for the first nine months remained at US$19.42 billion.
The domestic market maintained stable growth. Total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue in the first nine months increased by 13.4% compared to the same period last year. The percentage of businesses applying e-commerce reached 61%. In the energy sector, the power capacity reserve ratio reached approximately 25.97%, 4.17 percentage points higher than the 21.8% figure.
Based on the results of the first nine months, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has updated its growth scenario for the end of 2026. Accordingly, the average growth rate of the industrial production index in the remaining months of the year is expected to reach approximately 12.5 - 13%, ensuring that the whole year falls within the target range of 12 - 14%.
