articles.title: What ASEAN Mediation Can and Cannot Do - fulcrum.sg
articles.summary: What ASEAN Mediation Can and Cannot Do  fulcrum.sg
articles.full_text:
ASEAN@60: Special Edition
What ASEAN Mediation Can and Cannot Do
Published
Melinda Martinus and Fannesa Adisty Laksmita argue that ASEAN's strength lies in convening and facilitating dialogue but that without follow-through, different parties' political will and sufficient leverage, its mediation efforts will struggle to deliver results.
Today’s increasingly contested geopolitical environment is placing new strains on ASEAN’s longstanding diplomatic practices. As one of the world’s most established regional organisations, ASEAN has traditionally relied on quiet diplomacy, non-interference, consultation and consensus-building to manage differences among its diverse membership. These principles also shape its approach to conflict mediation, which favours dialogue and facilitation over direct intervention.
This approach can be effective when parties are willing to engage, but whether it produces concrete results depends on their willingness to cooperate and, in some cases, on ASEAN’s ability to influence their behaviour. Three cases illustrate different constraints and are worth examining: Indonesia’s use of shuttle diplomacy since the 1980s shows the gap between agreement and implementation; the ASEAN Special Envoy mechanism on Myanmar shows the limits of political will; and the ASEAN Chair’s role in the recent Cambodia-Thailand conflict shows the importance of leverage.
Indonesia’s shuttle diplomacy is one of the clearest manifestations of ASEAN’s preference for quiet engagement. In the late 1980s, then Foreign Minister Mochtar Kusumaatmadja travelled to Ho Chi Minh City to bring Cambodian factions and external parties together, culminating in the Jakarta Informal Meeting. This series of meetings contributed to the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements, which marked the end of the Cambodian-Vietnamese War. A similar approach was used again in 2012, when ASEAN foreign ministers failed to issue a joint communiqué over disagreements on the South China Sea dispute. In response, then-Foreign Minister Marty Natalegawa travelled to several ASEAN capitals within 36 hours to engage member states individually. His efforts contributed to the adoption of the ASEAN Six-Point Principles on the South China Sea, which reaffirmed respect for international law and the peaceful resolution of disputes.
However, shuttle diplomacy has been less successful when agreement had to be turned into action. In 2011, Indonesia helped mediate the Thailand–Cambodia border dispute by facilitating talks and seeking to establish an ASEAN role in managing the conflict. Although both sides agreed in principle to ASEAN observers, the mission stalled over its terms of reference, particularly Thailand’s conditions on the withdrawal of Cambodian troops.
These experiences show both the promise and limits of shuttle diplomacy. It can preserve ASEAN unity and create space for a common position when formal consensus-building falters. But diplomatic convergence does not necessarily translate into implementation. Where parties cannot agree on the terms required to put an arrangement into practice, even sustained engagement can reach an impasse.
ASEAN’s Special Envoy mechanism on Myanmar illustrates a different kind of limitation. Since the 2021 coup, six successive ASEAN Chairs – Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia and the current Chair, the Philippines – have each appointed a Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair on Myanmar to advance the Five-Point Consensus. Yet independent assessments have frequently characterised the mechanism as more symbolic than substantive. Its effectiveness has been constrained by the annual rotation of the Chairmanship, which disrupts continuity and established relationships, and by the absence of mechanisms to ensure that commitments are met.
The deeper problem, however, lies in the nature of the conflict itself. Unlike an interstate dispute, in which the parties may seek to contain tensions while preserving the existing political order, Myanmar is a civil war between different intra-state actors over political power. The military has limited incentives to negotiate an arrangement that could weaken its hold on power, while resistance groups have increasingly developed their own political and territorial positions. Under these conditions, a mediator can facilitate dialogue, convey messages, calibrate language and keep channels of communication open, but it cannot persuade the involved parties in the civil war to accept a negotiated settlement.
The recent Cambodia-Thailand conflict illustrates a related but distinct constraint: the absence of leverage. Despite several attempts by Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Malaysia’s capacity as ASEAN Chair last year to facilitate dialogue and de-escalation between Cambodia and Thailand, ASEAN’s efforts were limited by its lack of political or economic tools to influence either side into changing its position. Late last year, China’s Special Envoy for Asian Affairs, Deng Xijun, travelled between Cambodia and Thailand as part of Beijing’s own shuttle diplomacy to facilitate de-escalation following renewed armed confrontation. China’s involvement came after a US-brokered peace arrangement had struggled to produce a durable settlement. While ASEAN could provide a forum for dialogue and encourage restraint, it lacked the political and economic leverage needed to meaningfully influence the parties’ strategic calculations. Beijing, by contrast, possesses significant economic, political and strategic relationships with both Cambodia and Thailand, giving it greater capacity to encourage de-escalation and sustain diplomatic engagement.
Taken together, these cases show that ASEAN’s ability to convene and facilitate does not automatically translate into outcomes. This gap is becoming more consequential as Southeast Asians expect ASEAN to respond more quickly to crises in an increasingly contested strategic environment. The 2026 State of Southeast Asia Survey by the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute found that 34.7 per cent of respondents saw ASEAN’s slow response as an impediment to the region’s ability to respond to rapidly evolving political developments. Meanwhile, 32.2 per cent were concerned that ASEAN could become an arena for major-power competition, with Southeast Asian countries becoming proxies for competing external powers.
These experiences suggest four areas where ASEAN could strengthen its conflict-mediation capacity without abandoning the principles that underpin its diplomacy. First, ASEAN needs greater institutional continuity in mediation. Special envoys should not have to rebuild relationships and knowledge from scratch with each change of Chairmanship. A stronger support structure within the ASEAN Secretariat could preserve records and lessons, allowing successive Chairs to build on, rather than restart, existing processes.
Second, ASEAN should strengthen its capacity for preventive diplomacy. Much of the organisation’s diplomatic attention is mobilised only after violence has escalated. ASEAN could develop clearer procedures for identifying emerging tensions and deploying quiet diplomacy, fact-finding missions or good offices before disputes become harder to contain.
Third, mediation needs stronger follow-through. The 2011 Thailand-Cambodia experience shows that political agreement about a mechanism does not guarantee its implementation, while Myanmar demonstrates the difficulty of relying on commitments without effective means of monitoring progress. Despite challenging, ASEAN should at least place greater emphasis on agreed terms of reference, timelines, reporting arrangements and regular reviews when establishing such mechanisms. These measures would not require ASEAN to impose settlements, but they would make diplomatic commitments harder to leave unimplemented.
Fourth, ASEAN should be more deliberate about working with external partners when it lacks leverage. As the Cambodia-Thailand case shows, major powers may possess political, economic or strategic relationships that ASEAN lacks. Rather than treating external involvement as inherently at odds with ASEAN centrality, the bloc should establish clearer principles for complementary engagement, in which external actors provide resources, technical expertise or diplomatic leverage while ASEAN retains its convening and coordinating role. The objective should be for external involvement to support a regional process rather than displace it.
The policy challenge, therefore, is not to turn ASEAN into a conventional mediator with influence it does not possess, but to make better use of its existing diplomatic tools by making them more systematic, continuous and capable of producing follow-through. ASEAN’s strength lies in its ability to bring governments together and provide a politically acceptable regional platform. These roles may sometimes be underestimated, but they will only grow in importance as the region’s conflicts grow in complexity in the future.
Editor’s Note:
ASEANFocus+ articles are timely and critical insight pieces published by the ASEAN Studies Centre. The ASEAN@60 Special Edition series marks the organisation’s 60th anniversary in 2027 and highlights the key issues that will shape ASEAN and Southeast Asia as the organisation enters its seventh decade.
Melinda Martinus is a Fellow at the ASEAN Studies Centre, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.
Fannesa Adisty Laksmita is a Research Officer in the Indonesia Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

articles.title: IMF sees Malaysian GDP growth at 5.2% in 2026, 4.7% in 2027 - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: IMF sees Malaysian GDP growth at 5.2% in 2026, 4.7% in 2027  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 15): Malaysia’s gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow by 5.2% in 2026 and 4.7% in 2027, amid regional economic uncertainty, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
In its October 2026 Regional Economic Outlook for Asia and the Pacific, themed “Resilient Amid Uncertainty: Can It Be Sustained?”, the IMF highlighted technology-related exports and strong investment in data centres as key contributors to growth across the region.
“Malaysia and Singapore have increased exports as assemblers and packagers of technology products, while strong investment in data centres in China, India, Japan, Indonesia and Malaysia has also contributed to growth,” it said in the report on Thursday.
The investment in data centres has generated broader demand for intermediate goods from regional suppliers, including Thailand and Vietnam.
In Malaysia, operational data centre capacity stood at more than 1,000 megawatts (MW), with more than 1,500 MW under construction, according to the report.
“As for the composition of services exports, modern services in Malaysia accounted for about 30% of total services exports in 2023, while traditional services made up the remainder.
“Across Asean, services exports embodied in goods exports accounted for 17%, while services exports delivered through a commercial presence accounted for 30%,” the report said.
However, the IMF noted that many services exports in the region remain oriented towards global rather than regional markets, particularly modern services, of which only 14%, on average, are exported to countries within the Asia-Pacific region.
On inflation, the report said the pass-through of higher energy prices to both headline and core inflation had remained relatively contained in most advanced and emerging market economies.
“This was partly due to reliance on inventories and the widespread use of price-smoothing measures, including in Malaysia, [South] Korea and Thailand,” it added.
Containing the pass-through of higher energy prices has been the main policy objective, with more than 80% of economies adopting measures to limit the impact on domestic prices, using an average of two to four instruments.
These measures included fuel or utility price freezes and subsidies in Malaysia, alongside fuel tax and duty reductions in Cambodia and Laos, and subsidy-backed fuel price caps in Japan and Thailand.
Targeted support has also complemented broader measures to channel relief to exposed sectors and households. These included credit guarantees or liquidity facilities in Malaysia, India and Singapore.
Demand-side measures, such as work-from-home arrangements, shorter public sector hours and travel restrictions, have also been implemented in Malaysia and several other economies in the region.
On domestic demand, the IMF pointed out that Malaysia’s per capita consumption had grown faster than income, with a higher differential than the average among emerging market and developing economies, aided by a notable increase in household borrowing from banks.
For economies where consumption growth was relatively robust, including Malaysia and Thailand, the IMF said policies should focus on strengthening the resilience of consumption, particularly among vulnerable and highly indebted households.

articles.summary: Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen's Aden  CNAYemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport  Al JazeeraMissiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu  The Straits TimesIran-aligned Houthis launch deadly attack on Yemeni presidential palace in escalating campaign against Saudi Arabia  CNNIran-aligned Houthis target Yemeni presidential palace, prime minister remains unharmed...

ADEN, Yemen: The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday (Oct 15) on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government's interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.
The attack hit command centres located inside the presidential compound used by government forces and the Saudi-led military coalition that supports them, a Yemeni minister said on condition of anonymity.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government it backs have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.
Government military sources in Yemen said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in Thursday's strikes on Aden's Al-Maashiq palace in the divided country's south.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani had been present at the time, but "was not harmed in any way".
The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces with three missiles, and another for Saudi-led coalition forces at the complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.
Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them".
Yemen's civil war - in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 - reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.
Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.
Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," said Dr. Rayed Krimly.
The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.
Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired "several ballistic missiles" at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
OMAN MEETING REFUSED
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.
Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times this month.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
He added the group had "worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors", saying they now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.

articles.title: US Republicans, Democrats want Trump to reverse course on Russia diesel - Yahoo
articles.summary: US Republicans, Democrats want Trump to reverse course on Russia diesel  YahooCommentary: Trump’s Russian diesel U-turn comes at bad time for Ukraine  CNAJoe Scarborough Scorches Trump For Abandoning Ukraine, ‘Getting In Bed With Vladimir Putin’  Yahoo News SingaporeUkraine's Zelenskiy blasts US-Russian diesel deal, welcomes bigger European role in peace process  The Straits TimesKremlin says Russia restarts diesel exports after deal with Trump  ...
articles.full_text:
By Jan Wolfe and Patricia Zengerle
Oct 11 (Reuters) - Republican and Democratic US senators called on President Donald Trump on Sunday to "reverse course" on his diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it runs counter to US law barring imports of energy until Russia ends its aggression against Ukraine.
"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's brutal war against Ukraine," the seven senators - four of Trump's fellow Republicans and three Democrats - said in a statement.
They also said that the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation of its decision, something also required by law.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," the statement said.
It was only the latest bipartisan criticism of Trump's deal, a shift from his party's near-unanimous support for Trump's foreign policy decision weeks before November 3 midterm elections that will determine whether his Republicans will retain their control of Congress.
It was issued by Republican Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ron Wyden of Oregon.
Tillis had said earlier on Sunday that the diesel deal may be illegal and would put American lives at risk.
Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.
"I do believe there's a legitimate case for saying the president's not following the law," Tillis, who is retiring from the Senate in January, told NBC's "Meet the Press."
Prices for diesel — used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking — are near record highs and could hurt Republicans in next month's congressional elections.
Analysts have said that Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices.
ADMINISTRATION DEFENDS PACT
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the Trump administration will follow through with the deal using existing legal authority, and the agreement was good for the American people and would bring prices down.
"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says whether it's an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong," Bessent told "Fox & Friends."
Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," to honor the South Carolina Republican and longtime Russia hawk who died in July.
Some other Republicans had also criticized the diesel plan. Retiring Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska said on X on Friday that "propping up Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities."
Mike Pence, Trump's former vice president, called his decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil a "betrayal" of Graham's legacy and urged the president to "rescind" it.
As Trump's poll numbers have cratered, congressional Republicans have increasingly distanced themselves from the president, on matters ranging from the conflict in Iran to the trade war with Canada.
But the Senate's No. 2 Republican, John Barrasso of Wyoming, defended the diesel pact, telling CBS' "Face the Nation" that Trump is focused on bringing costs down.
"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in a call on Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy made it clear that the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe," his office said in a statement.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" taking effect immediately, but did not elaborate.
Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details of that agreement.
"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well," Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app.
There was no word from Moscow on the announcement, which followed days of US pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
(Reporting by Jan Wolfe and Patricia Zengerle; Additional reporting by Ismail Shakil; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Susan Fenton, Bill Berkrot and Mark Porter)

Agencies
Canada and Singapore are among the countries that remain committed to strengthening trade ties with China, despite growing global fragmentation and a push by governments towards greater self-sufficiency, officials from both countries said on Wednesday at an economic forum inNew Delhi.
Canada’s minister of international trade Maninder Sidhu said China was the country’s second-largest trading partner and highlighted opportunities for cooperation in areas where the two economies had complementary strengths, including China’s technology and Canada’s agricultural sectors.
"If you look at what China has in terms of energy storage technologies, that’s where Canada is very interested,” Sidhu said in a panel discussion titled "The Self-Sufficiency Scramble” at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, held in New Delhi from Tuesday to Thursday.
"There are key areas where we have partnerships with China we continue to build on,” he said, pointing to Canada’s agricultural sector that supplied "a great deal of canola or beef”, among other products, to the Chinese market.
Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, also minister for trade and industry, echoed that view, saying countries needed to maintain economic ties at a time when geopolitical tensions were increasingly dividing the global economy.
"It’s important for countries in the world to continue to engage with one another, even as the world has become increasingly fragmented,” Gan said, reaffirming the city state’s commitment to collaborating with China.
"Singapore and China will continue to have a very good working relationship. We continue to have a very strong economic cooperation in all aspects of the economy.” Gan said, adding that Singapore also collaborated strategically with other countries, such as India, in areas including semiconductors.
Their remarks underscored the difficulties of disentangling global supply chains that are deeply interconnected, even as trade disruption, geopolitical frictions and concerns over economic security push governments to reduce their dependence on foreign suppliers and seek self-sufficiency. Sunil Bharti Mittal, founder and chairman at Bharti Enterprises, an Indian multinational conglomerate headquartered in New Delhi, cautioned against overreliance on a single source – such as China – for critical supply chains.
"For a long period of time, I think the world let China become very strong in almost everything, from pharmaceuticals to the most critical components of the automobiles to electronics,” Mittal said at a separate forum panel held on Wednesday.
"Everybody is very happy that China produces high quality at low cost,” Mittal said, adding that interdependencies were becoming a "big question mark”.
Piyush Goyal, India’s commerce and industry minister, argued that technological capabilities would not remain concentrated in a handful of economies indefinitely. He said that developing alternative supply chains would require cooperation, rather than each country attempting to replicate an entire industrial ecosystem.
"I don’t think technology will remain the reserve of only one or a few countries.” Some countries could contribute talent, others specialised in equipment or components, while still others could provide the products and services needed to support commercial development, he added.
Goyal said that India was open to all countries around the world as long as the geopolitical situation did not deteriorate. Though there were past concerns related to China, he said, the two countries were currently working on developing their relations.

HONG KONG SAR – Media OutReach Newswire – 13 October 2026 – On October 13, the CICC Global Institute (CGI) held its 2026Q4 Macro Forum in Bangkok, Thailand, under the theme "China's Economy amid Global Rebalancing: New Paradigms and New Industries". The forum featured welcome remarks, keynote speeches, two thematic dialogues and an evening discussion session.
Yanliang Miao, Chief Economist and Senior Managing Director of CICC, shared his insights on China's economic transformation and the evolving international monetary order in his opening remarks and keynote speech. He noted that understanding China requires a global rebalancing perspective, considering both the dynamism of emerging industries and the implications of the transition from old to new growth engines for jobs, incomes and demand. Alongside its green and digital transitions, China is also working toward a growth model supported by higher household incomes and services-led consumption. Turning to the international monetary order, he observed that shifts in the global economy, trade networks and financial technology are driving the evolution toward a more diversified international monetary system. Economic and trade strength do not automatically translate into international currency status: institutional credibility and the depth and breadth of financial markets remain central to understanding this evolution and the internationalization of the renminbi.
Huimin Wu, Executive Dean of CICC Global Institute and Deputy Head of Research Department at CICC, noted that, as discussed in The New Pattern of Dual Circulation, a book jointly published this year by CICC Global Institute and CICC Research Department, China's economy is entering a new stage of development. Its trade and outward investment are undergoing a paradigm shift, while emerging industries are becoming increasingly important drivers of growth in the global economy. These changes are both part of the broader process of global economic rebalancing and deeply shaped by it, giving rise to a new pattern of interaction between China and the global economy.
The forum brought together experts and industry representatives from institutions including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO), Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF) at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, National University of Singapore, ICBC Standard Bank, Wood Mackenzie, and NSQ Capital. Discussions focused on the transformations of China's trade and outward investment and their global implications, as well as the prospects for emerging industries such as innovative pharmaceuticals, green energy, and artificial intelligence.
This marked the first time the CGI Quarterly Macro Forum was held in Southeast Asia. Taking place during the week of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings, amid international discussions on global economic opportunities and challenges, the event brought Chinese perspectives to the global conversation and offered Chinese insights into key issues concerning China's economy that are of broad international interest.
As an important part of CGI's ongoing efforts to strengthen international exchanges, present China's perspective, and foster a deeper understanding of China's economic transformation process, the event was an innovative exploration. Looking ahead, CGI will continue to deepen its international engagement and work toward building an international dialogue platform focused on China's economy, contributing to greater mutual trust and consensus, and playing a positive role in this cause.

articles.title: Limits of Philippines’ growth story - Manila Bulletin
articles.summary: Limits of Philippines’ growth story  Manila Bulletin
articles.full_text:
Philippines’ macroeconomic strategy for years relied on this sequence: foreign capital builds the infrastructure, overseas workers send home money to fuel consumption, and consumer spending keeps gross domestic product (GDP) expanding at a pace that makes neighboring economies envious.
That engine has stalled.
A series of central bank reports and economic data released just this month show the broader structural slowdown, with foreign direct investment falling 23.9 percent in the first seven months of the year to $4.07 billion. Cash remittances from overseas workers hit a three-month low in August. The peso broke through a psychological floor, sliding to a record 63.06 against the United States (US) dollar on Oct. 15. GDP growth slumped to 2.3 percent in the second quarter, bringing first-half growth to just 2.6 percent.
Officials would always frame these figures as a temporary pause brought on by global headwinds like persistent US inflation, high oil prices, and conflict in the Middle East. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is now projecting Philippine growth will average 3.4 percent in 2026 before accelerating to 5.1 percent in 2027.
But looking closer at the numbers, the problem goes deeper than a rough patch in the global business cycle. The core assumptions driving the domestic economy are showing real wear.
Take FDI. Net equity capital placements—the fresh money international companies commit when building factories or setting up local operations—dropped to $675 million through July. Nonresidents curtailed intercompany borrowing, while existing businesses reinvested fewer earnings. Multinational boards, faced with elevated global interest rates and shifting supply chains, are opting to wait out uncertainty rather than deploy capital into high-cost, logistics-heavy markets. While lower interest rates worldwide could offer relief, money will only follow policy clarity, predictable power costs, and completed public infrastructure.
At the same time, the domestic consumer base is absorbing multiple hits. Headline inflation hit 7.2 percent in September, far above the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) target band. A record-weak peso compounds the pressure by raising the cost of imported fuel and staple foods.
Historically, household budgets turned to remittances as a shock absorber. That buffer is thinning. Cash transfers passing through banks slowed to a 1.9 percent year-on-year growth rate in August, totaling $3.03 billion. Beyond short-term shifts, research from Oxford Economics highlighted a long-term structural issue: 83 percent of overseas Filipino workers are concentrated in lower-paid service, domestic work, and caregiving occupations. Unlike India, which has increased its share of technology and executive emigrants, the Philippines remains heavily reliant on lower-wage labor abroad.
With prices high at home, families rely on these funds primarily for basic survival. BSP surveys show that over 98 percent of recipient households use remittance money directly for food and essential groceries. The proportion set aside for healthcare, education, and precautionary savings has dropped significantly. When remittance growth slows, household spending contracts immediately.
Central bank policymakers face a tough setup. Raising benchmark lending rates protects the peso and tempers inflation, but it also risks choking off domestic credit when corporate balance sheets are already stretched. Cutting rates to spur growth risks accelerating capital flight and weakening the currency further.
The IMF’s medium-term projection of a 5.1 percent rebound in 2027 rests on a gradual recovery in investor confidence and easing energy costs. Achieving that outcome requires more than waiting for external conditions to clear. The government needs to upgrade worker skills to capture higher-paying overseas and local roles, address structural bottlenecks in domestic power and food supplies, and deliver clear, predictable rules for long-term investments.
Without those structural adjustments, brief cyclical recoveries will keep running up against the same ceiling.

articles.title: DKG TranXact Announces Institutional Pilot Readiness Ahead of Hong Kong and Singapore FinTech Events - PR Newswire

articles.full_text:
Company to attend Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK 2026 and Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, inviting financial institutions to evaluate its capital markets operations platform.
TORONTO, Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DKG TranXact today announced that it is ready to begin structured institutional pilots of its capital markets operations platform. The company is inviting banks, asset managers, broker-dealers and other financial institutions to evaluate TranXact against defined operational workflows, with a focus on improving visibility, exception ownership and coordination across post-trade operations.
The announcement comes ahead of DKG TranXact's attendance at Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK 2026, taking place November 2–6, 2026, and Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, taking place November 18–20, 2026, at Singapore EXPO. The company will use these events to meet prospective pilot participants, demonstrate the platform and discuss institutional requirements with financial services and technology partners.
TranXact brings reconciliation issues, settlement blockers, exception management, approvals, operational evidence and reporting into a unified, role-based workspace. The platform helps front-office, middle-office, back-office, settlements and compliance teams understand what requires attention, who is responsible for the next action and what remains unresolved throughout the operating day.
"Our objective is simple: give financial institutions a clearer view of what needs attention, who owns the next step and what must be resolved," said Karthik Ganapathiraju, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of DKG TranXact. "We are ready to begin pilots with institutions that want to evaluate that approach against their own operational priorities. Our attendance in Hong Kong and Singapore gives us an opportunity to move those conversations toward practical, measurable engagements."
Operational Control Across Existing Infrastructure
TranXact is designed to complement an institution's existing trading and post-trade infrastructure. It serves as a control and coordination layer across workflows, bringing together operational issues, ownership, supporting evidence and reporting while existing source systems remain in place.
The platform's data workflow takes approved operational data through validation, mapping and normalization, preserves source lineage and links related records. This foundation supports role-based work queues, dashboards, reports and audit trails, connecting the information teams receive with the actions they need to complete.
Core Platform Capabilities
Within an agreed pilot scope, institutions can evaluate capabilities spanning operational data, daily workflow management and oversight:
- Data intake, validation and traceability. Bring approved operational data into a structured environment, map and normalize records, and retain visibility into their originating sources.
- Reconciliation and exception management. Bring reconciliation breaks and operational exceptions into coordinated workflows that support investigation, accountable ownership and resolution tracking.
- Settlement oversight and instruction management. Review settlement blockers and standing settlement instruction exceptions alongside the relevant operational records, supporting evidence and required actions.
- Role-based workspaces. Provide participating teams with views aligned to their responsibilities, helping users focus on relevant issues while maintaining a shared operational context.
- Approvals, evidence and audit activity. Organize supporting documents, approval workflows and activity records to preserve the context behind operational decisions.
- Analytics and reporting. Produce operational dashboards, reports and evidence packs to support management review and end-of-day oversight.
A Structured Path from Evaluation to Adoption
DKG TranXact's pilot approach gives institutions a controlled starting point for assessing the platform before considering broader deployment. Initial evaluations can use synthetic or client-approved sample data in a read-only environment, with selected workflows mapped into TranXact and assessed against an agreed baseline.
Each engagement will define participating teams, data requirements, workflow boundaries, deliverables and success criteria. Evaluation measures may include the time required to assign exception ownership, manual reporting effort, visibility into settlement blockers and the completeness of supporting evidence. Results will be assessed within the participating institution's agreed scope.
"A successful pilot starts with a specific operational problem and a clear way to assess progress," said Daniel Golverk, President of DKG TranXact. "We want institutions to see how TranXact fits into their daily work, how it supports handoffs between teams and where it can reduce manual effort. By agreeing on workflows and success criteria at the outset, we can give operations and technology leaders a concrete basis for deciding how to move forward."
Any progression to production connectivity or wider deployment will be separately scoped and subject to the institution's architecture, security, governance and procurement requirements, alongside agreed support arrangements and acceptance criteria.
Meet DKG TranXact in Hong Kong and Singapore
DKG TranXact is inviting financial institutions and prospective technology and implementation partners attending either event to arrange product demonstrations, operational workflow discussions and pilot-scoping meetings with the team.
These discussions will focus on identifying specific operational challenges, understanding institutional requirements and determining where a controlled pilot can provide useful evidence for an adoption decision.
Institutions interested in evaluating TranXact are encouraged to contact the company ahead of the events to discuss their priorities and arrange a meeting.
About DKG TranXact

Chinese parts, machinery and know-how remain deeply embedded in countries seeking to build manufacturing industries of their own
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.
But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.
A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.

articles.title: With an income of 40 million VND per month, how much should I borrow to buy a house safely? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: With an income of 40 million VND per month, how much should I borrow to buy a house safely?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to a US-based international financial institution, the total monthly principal and interest payments on a home loan should not exceed 30-35% of a family's actual income.
This was shared by Associate Professor Dr. Ngo Tri Long, an economic expert, at the seminar "Real Estate After the Boom" organized by Dan Viet Newspaper on the morning of October 15th.
Have house prices hit rock bottom yet? What should real estate businesses do to overcome difficulties during this market downturn? Should those with genuine housing needs and investors put their money on the market at this time? - These are the hot questions being raised about the current real estate market.
According to Associate Professor Ngo Tri Long, the most crucial point for homebuyers is knowing how much to borrow safely. He stated that the total monthly principal and interest payments should not exceed 30-35% of the family's actual income, as recommended by an international financial organization in the United States.
A family with an income of 40 million VND/month should pay off approximately 12-14 million VND in debt. If the debt repayment ratio exceeds 40% of income, the financial risk and debt repayment pressure will be very high. Buyers should have sufficient reserves to cover living expenses and debt repayments for at least 6 months, ideally 9-12 months. In addition, they should anticipate the risk of fluctuating interest rates and assess whether the family can handle the burden.
For example, if someone borrows 1.5 billion VND over 20 years at an interest rate of 10% per year, they would have to pay approximately 14.5 million VND per month. However, in the current context, actual lending interest rates are high.
If interest rates increase from 10% to 15% per year, the monthly installment payment will increase from approximately VND 14.5 million to VND 19.8 million, assuming a fixed interest rate for each term. Thus, while house prices may decrease, the burden of debt repayment will increase significantly.
"Homebuyers should prioritize financial security and avoid borrowing beyond their means just because they fear missing out on the opportunity to buy a home," Mr. Long advised.
You may also like
From the perspective of the regulatory agency, Ms. Hoang Thu Hang, Deputy Director of the Department of Housing and Real Estate Market Management ( Ministry of Construction ), believes that there is currently a significant difference between the prices of primary and secondary real estate.
While prices in the secondary market have shown signs of decreasing, direct selling prices from developers have not adjusted significantly. This is one of the reasons why market liquidity continues to be a challenge.
Notably, a drop in secondary real estate prices does not necessarily mean investors are selling at a loss. Because prices had previously risen to very high levels, some price reductions may simply be a decrease in expected profits.
It is impossible to accurately predict where the market 'bottom' will be.
According to Ms. Hang, the demand for housing remains very high. If there are suitable products in terms of location, quality, and financial capability, people are willing to make transactions. The problem is that the market currently lacks products that meet these conditions.
However, the advice from representatives of the Ministry of Construction to those who need to buy a house to live in is not to wait for prices to fall to the "bottom" for too long, because it is very difficult to determine exactly when the market will hit rock bottom.
"Instead of simply hoping to buy a house at the lowest price, buyers need to assess whether the current price reflects the property's true value, price fluctuations over the years, and their own financial capabilities," Ms. Hang said.
You may also like
For example, a 70 m² apartment that previously cost around 3 billion VND has increased to 7 billion VND after several years. Buyers need to consider whether this increase is reasonable compared to market developments and the actual value of the apartment before making a decision.
However, those who buy real estate for investment purposes, without a need for actual residence, should continue to monitor market developments before making a decision.
According to Ms. Hang, buyers need to proactively assess their needs, financial capabilities, and acceptable price range, instead of relying entirely on market trend forecasts.
In particular, in the context of policies aimed at curbing speculation, market participants need to be more cautious with decisions regarding the use of financial leverage, avoiding expectations that real estate prices will continue to rise as they did in the previous period.

The 2026 Singapore Grand Prix attracted far more than Formula 1 fans, with billionaires, global chief executives and cryptocurrency industry leaders descending on the city-state for a series of major international business conferences. Singapore has increasingly used the excitement surrounding the Marina Bay race to strengthen its position as a global financial and business destination, with more than 40 corporate events taking place during this year’s Grand Prix period.
According to the Singapore Tourism Board, the number of business events organised around the Formula 1 weekend has risen considerably. More than 40 were held in 2026, compared with over 25 in 2025 and more than 30 in 2024. The growing overlap between motorsport, international finance and the cryptocurrency sector illustrates how Singapore is turning its annual Grand Prix into an economic opportunity that extends well beyond the circuit.
Singapore GP attracts global CEOs, billionaires and crypto industry leaders
Among the high-profile gatherings scheduled alongside the Singapore Grand Prix were the Milken Institute Asia Summit, TOKEN2049, the Forbes Global CEO Conference, the Solana Summit APAC and the Global-Asia Family Office Summit.
These conferences brought together senior figures from international finance, technology, investment and the cryptocurrency industry, creating a concentration of influential business visitors during one of Singapore’s busiest sporting weeks.
The strategy allows the city-state to capitalise on the international attention generated by Formula 1 while encouraging visitors to combine business commitments with the Grand Prix experience. For conference organisers, the presence of a major sporting event provides an additional attraction for delegates travelling from overseas.
The 2026 Singapore Grand Prix itself welcomed 301,294 spectators, making it the second-best attended edition in the event’s history. The figure demonstrates the continued appeal of the Marina Bay race, which has been a distinctive fixture on the Formula 1 calendar since its debut in 2008.
Formula 1 generates billions in tourism revenue for Singapore
The economic contribution of the Singapore Grand Prix has been substantial since the event first joined the Formula 1 World Championship.
Between its debut in 2008 and 2024, Formula 1 generated more than S$2.2 billion in incremental tourism receipts for Singapore. That represents an average of approximately S$150 million annually, compared with an estimated yearly cost of around S$140 million to organise the race.
The figures highlight the scale of the tourism activity associated with the Grand Prix, although the wider economic strategy increasingly involves attracting international conferences and business travellers alongside traditional motorsport visitors.
A particularly important component is the MICE sector, which covers meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions. This segment is becoming an increasingly significant contributor to Singapore’s tourism revenue.
In 2025, MICE tourism receipts increased by 35% to reach S$2.3 billion. That growth substantially exceeded the performance of the broader tourism industry, where receipts rose by 10% to a record S$32.8 billion.
Business-event visitors also spend considerably more on average than leisure tourists, making international conferences an especially valuable part of Singapore’s strategy to maximise the economic benefits of major events.
How Singapore uses Formula 1 to attract international business events
Singapore’s event organisers are becoming increasingly deliberate in their efforts to take advantage of the enthusiasm generated by Formula 1. By scheduling major conferences around the Grand Prix, they can encourage international delegates to extend their stays and participate in additional activities.
Poh Chi Chuan, executive director of exhibitions and conferences at the Singapore Tourism Board, explained that successful event planners recognise the opportunities created when a city is already attracting significant attention and their intended audience is travelling there.
According to Poh, the most effective organisers build on that existing momentum, using the excitement surrounding major events to create a natural attraction for business visitors.
The approach is particularly visible at TOKEN2049, one of the world’s leading cryptocurrency conferences, where international participation has continued to increase.
At the 2026 edition, overseas visitors accounted for 85.6% of attendees, compared with 82.7% in 2025. The figures demonstrate the event’s increasingly international character and its ability to attract participants from across the global cryptocurrency industry.
Chinese delegates represented 11.8% of total attendance, almost double the 6% recorded the previous year. This increase meant that Chinese participants overtook Americans to become the largest national group attending the conference.
The growth illustrates how the combination of international business conferences and the Singapore Grand Prix is helping the city-state attract an increasingly diverse audience of senior executives, investors and technology-sector representatives.
Singapore GP drives strong demand for luxury hotels
The influx of international business travellers has also produced exceptionally strong demand across Singapore’s luxury hotel sector, particularly around Marina Bay.
Marina Bay Sands operated at almost full occupancy during the Grand Prix week while simultaneously hosting TOKEN2049 at its convention centre. The combination demonstrates how major business conferences and international sporting events are increasingly overlapping, with hotels and conference facilities benefiting from both audiences.
The impact on accommodation prices was already evident in October 2025, when the concentration of MICE events and Formula 1 activities contributed to a sharp increase in hotel rates.
Average room prices rose by 19.5% compared with the previous year, reaching S$384.15. On the opening day of that Grand Prix weekend, hotel occupancy climbed to 95.9%, while the average room rate reached S$757.62.
These figures underline the commercial value of bringing together major conferences and the Singapore Grand Prix within the same period. Hotels benefit from high occupancy and stronger room rates, while the city attracts visitors whose spending extends across accommodation, hospitality and other tourism services.
Why the Singapore Grand Prix has become more than an F1 race
Since its introduction in 2008, the Singapore Grand Prix has developed into one of Formula 1’s most recognisable events. Its setting around the illuminated Marina Bay Street Circuit provides a distinctive backdrop for the championship, with the race taking place in the heart of a major international financial centre.
The 2026 Singapore Grand Prix weekend once again placed the city at the centre of international motorsport attention, while the accompanying business conferences attracted an additional audience of corporate decision-makers and investors.
For Singapore, the combination offers benefits that extend beyond ticket sales and the immediate spending of Formula 1 spectators. The Grand Prix helps generate international visibility, while the surrounding conferences encourage higher-spending visitors to remain in the city for longer.
The increasing number of business events, strong international attendance at TOKEN2049 and sustained demand for luxury accommodation all demonstrate how closely the sporting and corporate sides of the Singapore Grand Prix have become connected.
With more than 40 business gatherings coinciding with the 2026 race and MICE tourism already recording strong revenue growth, Singapore is continuing to strengthen a model in which Formula 1 serves not only as a major sporting attraction but also as a catalyst for international business and tourism.

articles.title: Vietnam's economy in Q4: Accelerating but not complacent about inflation. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam's economy in Q4: Accelerating but not complacent about inflation.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Chinhphu.vn) - Vietnam's economy entered the fourth quarter of 2026 with a GDP growth rate of 9.01% in the first nine months, creating a foundation for continued acceleration in the remaining months of the year. However, along with promoting investment, exports, and consumption, the economy needs to enhance domestic value and control inflationary pressures to maintain sustainable growth.
GDP in the third quarter of 2026 increased by 9.95%, continuing the positive growth trend. However, with the goal of achieving an annual GDP growth rate of 10% or higher, the final quarter of the year still places high demands on growth drivers, especially investment, production, and consumption.
Investment continues to be a notable driving force. Foreign direct investment (FDI) disbursed in the first nine months reached US$21.07 billion, a 12.1% increase year-on-year and the highest level for the same period in the past five years. Meanwhile, public investment disbursement by the end of September reached 62.9% of the plan assigned by the Prime Minister , indicating that a large amount of capital still needs to be disbursed in the remaining months.
Speaking with a reporter from the Government Online Newspaper, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, assessed that public investment and FDI continue to be two important drivers of GDP growth.
According to Mr. Giap, key infrastructure projects, especially those that enhance connectivity, if implemented effectively, will facilitate production and business activities.
However, accelerating disbursement must go hand in hand with improving the efficiency of capital utilization. Completion progress, the ability to put the project into operation, and the actual impact on the economy are decisive factors. Disbursement needs to be linked to project quality control and avoid scattered investments.
Besides investment, the domestic market continues to contribute significantly to growth. Total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue in the first nine months increased by 13.4% year-on-year; excluding price factors, the increase reached 7.8%.
Mr. Bui Minh Giap noted that a market of over 100 million people is a major advantage for Vietnam. Domestic consumption plays a crucial role alongside exports, especially in the fourth quarter – the peak shopping season. The development of e-commerce also opens up further opportunities to boost consumption.
Nevertheless, year-end consumer prospects remain dependent on employment, income, and consumer confidence. The discrepancy between retail sales growth at current prices and growth after price adjustments suggests a greater need to consider actual purchasing power.
With the cost of living under pressure to rise, people's spending power will directly impact the contribution of consumption to growth in the final months of the year.
Enhancing domestic value in the global value chain.
In the first nine months of 2026, merchandise exports reached US$434.3 billion, a 24.5% increase compared to the same period last year. However, imports increased by 36.7%, significantly higher than the export growth rate, resulting in a merchandise trade deficit of US$19.42 billion.
Imports primarily consist of production materials, reflecting the significant demand for machinery, equipment, and raw materials for manufacturing. This reality necessitates the development of domestic supply capacity and an increase in the localization rate.
The export structure also reveals significant disparities between economic sectors. The foreign-invested sector, including crude oil, accounts for 80.7% of total merchandise exports, while the domestic economic sector accounts for 19.3%.
You may also like
This proportion reflects the significant role of the FDI sector and also indicates the need to enhance the production capacity and participation in value chains of Vietnamese businesses.
Assessing the quality of foreign investment flows, Mr. Bui Minh Giap suggested that Vietnam should prioritize FDI projects that have the potential to create high added value, promote technology transfer, and create conditions for domestic businesses to participate more deeply in the supply chain.
According to the ADB's Chief Economist, the issue lies not only in the scale of capital attracted but also in the added value left for the economy and the ability to enhance the capacity of Vietnamese businesses.
To better capitalize on opportunities from the FDI sector, ADB experts also emphasized the need to increase investment in research and development (R&D), gradually master technology, and improve corporate governance and management capabilities.
Technology transfer does not happen automatically. Vietnamese businesses need to improve their capabilities to meet the requirements of foreign partners and demonstrate their ability to handle specific stages in the production chain. The government also needs to support and promote technological innovation and enhance business capacity.
Regarding exports, Mr. Bui Minh Giap believes that attention should be paid to the revenue generated rather than just focusing on the quantity of goods sold.
Export markets are increasingly demanding higher product quality, food safety, traceability, and product standards. Businesses need to improve their capacity to meet these requirements, linking increased export turnover with increased domestic value, and gradually participating more deeply in the global value chain.
Implement a prudent monetary policy and control inflation.
Along with the requirement to maintain high growth rates, price developments are creating additional pressure on macroeconomic management.
The average CPI for the first nine months of 2026 increased by 4.52% year-on-year; September alone saw a 5.08% increase compared to September 2025. The price index for raw materials, fuels, and production materials increased by 5.12% in the first nine months, reflecting the pressure of input costs on businesses.
Increased production costs can narrow profit margins and limit business expansion. If businesses pass on these increased costs to the selling price, consumer purchasing power will also be affected.
In its September 2026 report, the ADB projected Vietnam's inflation for the whole year at 4.3%. Price developments up to the end of September necessitate continued close monitoring of inflationary pressures in the final quarter of the year.
According to Mr. Bui Minh Giap, inflationary pressure in Vietnam is influenced by many external factors, including fluctuations in energy prices, logistics costs, and disruptions in the supply chain.
You may also like
To promote growth without putting further pressure on price levels, ADB experts emphasized the need to improve the quality of public investment, avoid spreading resources too thinly, and not pursue disbursement deadlines at all costs.
Monetary policy also needs to be managed cautiously, taking into account exchange rate movements, inflation, and credit quality.
Regarding the outlook for 2027, Mr. Bui Minh Giap believes that productivity will remain one of the major bottlenecks in the Vietnamese economy.
Boosting public investment and mobilizing resources can support immediate growth. However, to maintain high and sustainable growth rates, the economy needs to rely more on improving productivity and leveraging the role of the business sector.
ADB experts emphasized three key areas for focus: improving productivity; developing low-emission connectivity infrastructure; and enhancing business capacity and workforce skills.
During the acceleration phase in the fourth quarter, improving investment efficiency and controlling inflationary pressures are crucial requirements for maintaining growth momentum. In the long term, improving productivity, enhancing business capacity, and the quality of human resources will be the foundation for Vietnam's economy to maintain high growth in 2027 and beyond.

articles.summary: Which businesses benefit from increasingly selective capital flows?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Capital flows depend on credit outlooks among different groups of businesses (Illustrative image) | 
 While facing similar pressures on costs and capital mobilization, the credit outlook for Vietnamese businesses is evolving in different directions. Some sectors are supported by public investment and consumer demand, while those heavily reliant on debt financing or with weak cash flow face increasing debt repayment risks.
 Stable cash flow gives businesses an advantage.
 Within the group with an improving credit outlook, VIS Rating identified three sectors: oil and gas services, infrastructure operations, and tourism and resorts. Of these, infrastructure-related businesses and some oil and gas service businesses are receiving support from public investment.
 According to the report, public investment disbursement in the first seven months of 2026 reached US$16.3 billion, a 20% increase compared to the same period last year. This capital supports construction contractors, infrastructure businesses, and some oil and gas service companies, creating favorable conditions to boost business activities.
 However, the level of benefit varies among businesses. Aggregated data shows that large-scale construction contractors recorded stronger revenue growth than smaller-scale contractors. Differences in operational scale also reflect their ability to capitalize on opportunities from investment projects.
 Notably, VIS Rating emphasizes that improving a credit profile depends on the ability to convert revenue growth into cash flow. This means that increased revenue alone is not enough to guarantee debt repayment capacity if the business does not improve its cash collection process.
 For contractors, accelerating public investment only truly supports credit prospects when the ability to collect payments improves. This is a crucial condition for project revenue to become a source of funds to meet financial obligations. Besides oil and gas services and infrastructure operation, tourism and resort activities are also classified as having improving credit prospects.
 In the stable outlook group, the sectors mentioned include banking and securities, industrial park development, modern retail, and fast-moving consumer goods. Among these, large-scale banks, state-owned banks, and large domestic consumer goods enterprises are assessed as having relatively better resilience.
 For banks, the advantage lies in a solid deposit base, a diversified loan portfolio, and prudent credit granting standards. These factors help large and state-owned banks maintain more stable capital, liquidity, and asset quality compared to smaller banks.
 Resilience becomes even more important as credit growth continues to outpace deposit growth, increasing competition for capital. In this environment, the stability of deposit sources and the quality of the credit portfolio make the difference in the ability to cope with rising capital costs.
 For large-scale domestic consumer businesses, the credit outlook is supported by retail consumption growth, relatively high revenue forecasting capabilities, and low profit volatility. These factors help businesses maintain more stable cash flow in the face of business environment fluctuations.
 Thus, the advantage of businesses with promising and stable prospects stems not only from growth opportunities but also from their ability to maintain capital, control profit fluctuations, and generate cash flow to support business operations.
 Which sectors are under the greatest pressure?
 Conversely, residential real estate, automobiles, and export businesses with low profit margins are classified as having a worsening credit outlook. Among these, residential real estate is the sector with the most significant debt repayment and refinancing risks.
 Data shows that real estate transactions nationwide in the second quarter of 2026 decreased by 36% compared to the same period last year. In Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, the primary apartment absorption rate decreased from 95% in 2025 to 73%.
 Weak sales, rising interest expenses, and slow project implementation are directly impacting businesses' ability to generate cash flow. Projects facing legal obstacles are also struggling with sales and product delivery.
 According to VIS Rating, the risks are concentrated in businesses with weak operating cash flow, reliance on the secondary market, and the need for refinancing through bond issuance. Issuers with a history of defaulting on or extending bond payments, and with limited bank credit relationships, may face greater difficulties in accessing new funding.
 Conversely, businesses with ongoing projects, clear handover schedules, and strong relationships with banks are considered to have better access to credit. This differentiation therefore occurs not only between industries but also within the real estate sector itself.
 For small-scale export businesses, the pressure comes from uncertain market demand, the risk of increased tariffs from the US, and high energy and transportation costs. The sectors mentioned include textiles, footwear, and wood products.
 The ability to pass on increased costs to customers is limited, while market diversification is difficult, leaving small businesses more vulnerable. Airlines are also under pressure from high fuel costs.
 The overall context continues to pose challenges to debt repayment capacity. Domestic retail fuel prices increased by 19-52% year-on-year, the CPI rose by 4.9%, and the average CPI for the first eight months of 2026 increased by 4.5%. Rising operating costs are weakening cash flow, while inflationary pressures limit the room for monetary policy easing.
 The report forecasts that lending interest rates will remain high in the near future. As banks become more selective in lending, businesses with weak credit profiles and limited access to funding will face greater pressure in securing working capital and refinancing.
 The outlook could improve if the gap between credit growth and deposit mobilization narrows, the cost of capital decreases, and business cash flow recovers. Specifically for real estate, sales, handover progress, and the resolution of legal obstacles are crucial factors in strengthening debt repayment sources.
 Conversely, if operating and financing costs continue to rise, export conditions deteriorate, or projects are delayed, debt repayment and refinancing risks will increase, especially for businesses with weak financial foundations.
 According to VIS Rating's assessment, bank credit and bonds will increasingly favor issuers with strong credit profiles. In this environment, the ability to maintain stable cash flow and access to capital becomes a decisive factor in differentiating credit outlooks among businesses.

| Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Gia Túc (centre) at the US-Việt Nam Business Summit 2026 in Hà Nội on Wednesday. — VNA/VNS Photos | 
HÀ NỘI — Việt Nam has identified five priority areas for cooperation with the US, Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Gia Túc said on Wednesday. They include high technology, particularly semiconductors, artificial intelligence and data; clean energy; sustainable supply chains; finance and innovation; and education and training.
The sectors are expected to create business opportunities in both countries while helping Vietnam strengthen its production capacity, technological capabilities and integration into global supply chains, Túc told the US-Việt Nam Business Summit 2026 in Hà Nội.
After 30 years of diplomatic relations and more than three years since the two countries established a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, bilateral ties have made significant progress, laying the groundwork for expanded economic, trade and investment cooperation, he said.
Achievements include stronger dialogue and mutual trust, improved cooperation frameworks, closer trade and investment ties and advances in technology cooperation.
The two countries are working to conclude negotiations on a reciprocal trade agreement aimed at ensuring fairness and balance, which would provide businesses with a stable, transparent and predictable framework for investment and long-term cooperation, Túc said.
Economic ties are increasingly extending beyond goods trade to business partnerships, production linkages and deeper integration into each other's supply chains. Stronger connections would help increase local value and foster long-term partnerships between the two countries' business communities, he added.
Expanding cooperation with the US aligns with Việt Nam's long-term development strategy, which focuses not only on boosting trade and investment but also on improving growth quality, increasing domestic value-added commerce and strengthening business ties in technology, manufacturing and innovation, Túc said.
| Representatives from US companies at the event. | 
Scope to deepen investment ties
Bilateral trade between Việt Nam and the US reached US$157.83 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 24.5 per cent from a year earlier. The US ranks 11th among 153 countries and territories investing in Việt Nam.
The growing presence and investment of major US companies in Việt Nam, such as HP, NVIDIA, FedEx and Excelerate Energy, brings capital, technology and management expertise while creating opportunities for Vietnamese firms to join supply chains and strengthen their capabilities, said vice chairman of the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) Nguyễn Quang Vinh.
However, US investment in Việt Nam still fails to reflect American businesses' potential fully, Vinh said, calling on both governments to maintain a stable, transparent, and predictable policy environment and strengthen public-private dialogue to address obstacles to trade and investment.
He also urged the two countries to promote balanced, mutually beneficial trade by improving access for Vietnamese goods to the US market while expanding opportunities for Việt Nam to import US products, technology, equipment, and services.
US companies, particularly those with advanced technological capabilities and substantial investment resources, should expand their investment in Việt Nam in both scale and quality, with a long-term focus on high value-added activities, he said.
Vinh called for stronger bilateral cooperation between the two countries' business communities in artificial intelligence, digital technology, semiconductors, energy, and the green transition, as well as more opportunities for Vietnamese companies to participate in supply chains, joint production, and research and development.
Vietnamese businesses, meanwhile, should improve their competitiveness, adopt international standards, upgrade technology and management capabilities and seek more trade and investment opportunities in the US, he said.
VCCI said it would continue working with the American Chamber of Commerce in Việt Nam (AmCham Vietnam) and the US Chamber of Commerce to identify cooperation opportunities, help businesses address challenges and promote balanced and sustainable economic relations.
During the event, US Ambassador to Việt Nam Jennifer Wicks said American companies are willing to support Việt Nam's development goals and are seeking opportunities to increase investment and expand their operations in the country.
Attracting investment depends partly on a favourable legal framework with clear, predictable regulations developed through consultation with affected stakeholders, she said, adding that policy stability and transparency are essential to long-term business decisions.
Mark Gillin, chairman of the National Board of Governors of AmCham Vietnam, said the next phase of bilateral relations would depend on implementation and tangible results.
US businesses want to invest, expand operations and build long-term partnerships in Việt Nam. Still, the country needs to improve regulatory predictability, develop reliable infrastructure, ensure access to energy and skilled workers, and translate policy commitments into concrete outcomes, Gillin said.
For his part, John Goyer, executive director of Southeast Asia at the US Chamber of Commerce, said Việt Nam is becoming an increasingly important partner for American businesses and a key participant in the next phase of economic cooperation in Southeast Asia. — VNS

The 2nd session of the 16th National Assembly, which opened on October 17th and is expected to last 28 working days, will consider and approve 43 draft laws and normative legal resolutions.
On the afternoon of October 16th, at the National Assembly building, the National Assembly Office held a press conference on the proposed agenda for the 2nd Session of the 16th National Assembly. Member of the Central Committee of the Party, Secretary General of the National Assembly, and Head of the National Assembly Office, Le Quang Manh, chaired the press conference.
Attending the press conference were Vice Chairwoman of the Committee on Culture and Social Affairs Lo Thi Viet Ha; Vice Chairwoman of the Committee on Science, Technology and Environment Nguyen Phuong Tuan; Vice Chairwoman of the National Assembly Office Nguyen Van Hien; National Assembly member Tran Thi Kim Nhung, full-time member of the Committee on Law and Justice; National Assembly member Pham Thi Hong Yen, full-time member of the Committee on Economy and Finance; National Assembly member Hoang Nam Hai, full-time member of the Committee on Citizen Petitions and Supervision; along with representatives from the Standing Committee of the National Assembly and its Committees; and representatives from domestic and foreign news agencies and press.
According to the National Assembly's electronic portal, speaking at a press conference, the Secretary General of the National Assembly and Head of the National Assembly Office, Le Quang Manh, emphasized that the National Assembly will officially open its Second Session on October 17th. The session is expected to last approximately 28 working days and will be divided into two phases to ensure sufficient time for considering and deciding on the very large volume of work. To complete the planned agenda, the National Assembly plans to work on both Saturdays and Sundays.
At this session, the National Assembly is expected to consider and approve 43 legal documents and provide feedback on 4 draft laws. This aims to complete the legislative program, promptly concretizing the new policies, orientations, and requirements identified in the Central Committee's documents. At the same time, the National Assembly will consider and decide on 10 important groups of issues concerning socio-economic development, the state budget, supreme oversight, and matters within its jurisdiction.
The Secretary General of the National Assembly and Head of the National Assembly Office stated that, compared to previous sessions, the volume of laws and resolutions considered at this session is very large, placing very high demands on preparation and organization. In the context of increasingly diverse methods of accessing information, especially in the digital environment, the National Assembly Office hopes that press agencies will continue to promote innovation, improve the quality of information transmission, ensure accuracy, objectivity and responsibility, and meet the concerns of voters and the people nationwide.
Presenting a summary report on the proposed agenda for the 2nd Session of the 16th National Assembly, Deputy Head of the National Assembly Office Nguyen Van Hien stated that the 2nd Session of the 16th National Assembly will hold its preparatory session and opening ceremony on the morning of October 17, 2026; and is expected to close on November 21, 2026. The session is expected to last 28 working days, including 6 Saturdays and 1 Sunday; from November 15-19, the National Assembly will take a break to allow its agencies, the Government , and relevant agencies to review, revise, and finalize draft laws and resolutions.
Regarding the planned agenda and content of the session, Deputy Head of the National Assembly Office Nguyen Van Hien said:
