Regarding the consideration and decision-making on socio- economic issues, the state budget, oversight, and other important matters within its jurisdiction , the National Assembly will: Review the Report on the implementation of the socio-economic development plan for 2026 and the projected socio-economic development plan for 2027; decide on the socio-economic development plan for 2027. Review the implementation of the state budget for 2026; decide on the state budget estimates for 2027 and the central budget allocation plan for 2027; review the implementation of the public investment plan for 2026 and the projected public investment plan for 2027; decide on the public investment plan using state budget funds for 2027. Approve the final accounts of the state budget for 2025.
In addition, the National Assembly will consider the consolidated report of opinions and recommendations from voters and the people submitted to the Second Session of the 16th National Assembly. It will also review reports on the results of monitoring the resolution of voter petitions, receiving citizens, handling letters and petitions, and resolving complaints and denunciations from citizens, including: the report of the Standing Committee of the National Assembly on the results of monitoring the resolution of voter petitions submitted to the First Session of the 16th National Assembly; and the report of the Standing Committee of the National Assembly on the results of receiving citizens, handling letters and petitions, and monitoring the resolution of complaints and denunciations from citizens submitted to the National Assembly in 2026. Simultaneously, it will conduct interpellation and answer sessions; and consider and decide on other matters within its authority.

articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs advised Singaporeans to defer all travel to Saudi Arabia amid heightened security risks.
SINGAPORE: Some Singapore pilgrims are pressing ahead with plans to perform Umrah in Saudi Arabia despite an advisory to defer travel to the country, while others are weighing whether to postpone or even cancel their trips.
The Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) on Wednesday (Oct 14) advised Singaporeans planning to perform umrah to consider postponing their trips, in line with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' (MFA) advisory to defer all travel to Saudi Arabia amid heightened security risks.
The advisory comes amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, with recent missile and drone attacks affecting parts of Saudi Arabia, including airports.
Umrah is a voluntary pilgrimage to Mecca for Muslims and can be performed at any time of the year.
One family had their pilgrimage cancelled just hours before they were due to check in for their flight on Wednesday (Oct 14).
Mdm Hadijah, who was scheduled to travel with her family, said they were “heartbroken” when flight disruptions derailed their plans.
The family had planned to remain in the kingdom until Oct 25 as part of an Umrah trip with tour agency OneOasis Travel, but it was called off after their Emirates flight from Dubai to Saudi Arabia was cancelled.
“We are discussing with our family on postponing it to a later date, possibly next year. We hope and pray to make this Umrah trip come true,” said Mdm Hadijah, who declined to give her full name.
For others, preparations for their upcoming pilgrimages continue as they monitor developments.
Denise Deanna Chew is scheduled to travel from Nov 3 to Nov 13 with her husband and their two sons, aged 14 and one.
The family is travelling with And.i Experience and flying with Saudia Airlines.
Ms Chew said the advisories had made her concerned, particularly as she would be travelling with a baby.
For now, the family is taking a “wait-and-see” approach.
"We are continuing with our preparations, but at the same time, we are monitoring developments closely," Ms Chew said.
The family still intends to perform Umrah but Ms Chew said they are also mentally prepared for the possibility that the trip may not happen.
"I believe having faith doesn't mean disregarding safety or taking unnecessary risks," she said.
Ms Chew said the family would reconsider travelling if the situation worsens, if MFA or MUIS issues stronger advisories, or if their flights are cancelled.
Another pilgrim, who wanted to be identified only as Ms A, is due to travel with family and friends from Oct 21 to Nov 1, flying with Emirates.
She said she is aware of the potential security concerns but she still intends to proceed with the trip.
However, she said she would respect her travel agency's decision if it decides to cancel the trip.
"We are not in control of the situation," she said.
She added that the travel agency she is going with has been assuring her group that it is monitoring the situation closely.
Asked what might make her reconsider her plans, Ms A said she would still proceed with Umrah "should it be allowed".
Meanwhile, Nur Zhafirin Bin Nor Azhar, who is planning to perform his first Umrah this December, is hoping for the situation in the region to de-escalate soon.
“But if the travel agency deems it unsafe, then no choice but to follow,” he said.
      
            Related:
      
  
TRAVEL AGENCIES MONITORING DEVELOPMENTS
Travel agencies CNA spoke to said they are monitoring developments closely, with trips still scheduled to proceed.
A group with Noor Mohamad Services & Travel left Singapore for Jeddah on a direct Saudia Airlines flight on Wednesday and arrived in Mecca on Thursday morning.
Director Ustazah Juyda Noor Mohamad said the pilgrims had been communicating through a WhatsApp group ahead of their departure and were ready to proceed with the trip.
The agency said it took the MFA and MUIS advisories seriously.
"Our priority is the safety and well-being of our pilgrims, and our position is to encourage them to defer their journeys while security risks remain heightened," she said.
Another agency, Shahidah Travel, said all its Umrah departures remain on track, with no changes to its travel arrangements as of Wednesday.
The agency currently has a group in Mecca performing Umrah, with all its pilgrims in good condition.
It said it would continue to monitor flight schedules and coordinate with relevant parties, with any changes or disruptions communicated to affected pilgrims.
It has also registered its pilgrims through MFA's eRegister portal to facilitate communication and coordination if necessary.
As part of its emergency preparations, an appointed staff member would also carry copies of pilgrims' passports and passport-sized photographs.
Meanwhile, Travelconnect is reviewing upcoming departures with airlines and its ground operators in Saudi Arabia.
As of Wednesday, about 5 per cent of customers booked for year-end departures to Saudi Arabia had contacted the agency about either postponing or cancelling their trips, said its director Mohamed Nafis Rahman.
But some customers have also expressed a desire to proceed with their trips, he added.
"We understand their intentions but any decision to proceed must take into account the official advisories, flight availability and the safety of the ground arrangements," said Mr Nafis.
For pilgrims already in Saudi Arabia, tour leaders and ground operators are maintaining close contact with them, checking on their welfare and monitoring their return flights, he said.
Hamidah Travel & Tours told CNA on Wednesday that it planned to speak to its pilgrims following the advisory issued by MFA and MUIS.
The agency's director, Badruzzaman Abdul Majid, said it would continue to monitor the situation. If flight cancellations affect its pilgrims, the agency would arrange alternative flights.
The company had a group of pilgrims in Madinah as of Tuesday.
While agencies are monitoring the security situation and keeping upcoming departures under review, pilgrims who decide not to travel face another consideration: how much of what they have paid can they get back?
POSTPONING OR CANCELLING
A full refund is not guaranteed for pilgrims who postpone or cancel their trips, and some could incur additional fees.
Agencies said the financial implications would depend on arrangements with airlines, hotels and other service providers.
MUIS on Wednesday said it was engaging Umrah travel agents to encourage them to assist affected pilgrims with "clear information and, where possible, flexible arrangements for postponement or rescheduling".
Travel agencies told CNA, however, that the options available would depend in part on their airlines and other service providers.
Mr Badruzzaman said Hamidah Travel & Tours would have to work closely with airlines and other providers. For now, airlines are allowing postponements, although penalties could apply as flights are still operating.
The agency will assess the situation and discuss the options with pilgrims, he said. Its next group is scheduled to depart for Saudi Arabia on Oct 22.
If the situation deteriorates to the point where flights are no longer operating, however, the trip would have to be cancelled.
"We are here to help pilgrims. This is ‘amanah’ for us," Mr Badruzzaman said, referring to the responsibility to help pilgrims.
Travelconnect said it is reviewing postponement and refund options with its service providers.
Whether a full or partial refund is available will depend on each booking, including which payments can be recovered from airlines, hotels and other providers, Mr Nafis said.
As of Wednesday, none of the airlines Travelconnect was working with had offered refunds for customer-initiated cancellations.
The agency is seeking flexibility from airlines and hotels, including changes without additional charges where possible.
"We will explain the available options and any applicable costs to each affected customer before they make a decision," he said.
Travelconnect also strongly encourages customers to buy travel insurance, which Mr Nafis said almost all of its customers do.
Coverage, however, depends on the individual policy, and customers should check with their insurers about what is covered and excluded, particularly in relation to the current situation.
"Customers should not assume that all cancellations or disruptions related to the current situation are covered," he said.
Noor Mohamad Services & Travel said it would prioritise postponement or rescheduling, subject to availability and confirmation from its service providers.
For customers who request cancellation, the agency will assess each booking individually and explain the applicable refund arrangements.
The amount refundable will depend on the booking terms, payments already committed and any waivers or refunds secured from suppliers.
"We cannot promise a blanket full refund before these details are confirmed,” Ustazah Juyda said.
"Our aim is to minimise financial losses for our pilgrims and provide a clear breakdown of any amounts that cannot be recovered.”
The agency would seek flexibility from its airline and hotel partners, including changes without penalties where possible, she added.

KUALA LUMPUR – Up every morning at 4am to prepare his kitchen for two shifts, 52-year-old Chef Teddy is no stranger to hard work. He runs Dapur Warisan in Puncak Jalil, on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, from 9am to midnight daily. But as transboundary haze blankets the area, he is finding that no amount of effort, however gruelling, can outpace the polluted air.
Daily sales at his Chinese Muslim restaurant have plunged by 30% from their usual RM4,500 (S$1,410), with mid-October marking his worst business period since the haze began about a month ago. He said he might have to take drastic action if the situation does not improve.
“I’m considering laying off staff and cutting operating hours to keep the cafe running,” Teddy, who did not want to give his full name, told The Straits Times.
His struggle mirrors a growing crisis for business owners across Malaysia, who are facing weaker sales, rising operating costs and mounting cash-flow pressures because of the haze.
The haze is fuelled by forest and peatland fires in Indonesia, particularly in Sumatra and Kalimantan, during the region’s dry season. In 2026, prolonged dry conditions linked to El Nino, a climate pattern that can bring hotter, drier weather to much of South-east Asia, have worsened the fires. The ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre warned that dry conditions will intensify through November, raising the risk of a lengthy disruption.
The economic strain spans multiple sectors. Sunway Lagoon, an outdoor theme park in Selangor, has seen a 50% to 60% drop in visitors since the haze began.
“Parents have concerns over the general well-being of the family,” a spokesperson said, noting the park has temporarily suspended part-time retiree workers, cleared employee annual leave and moved up annual ride maintenance to manage operations during the slowdown.
Farther south in Johor state, 36-year-old farmer Tan Chee Kiong is battling the same atmospheric blanket at his 73ha vegetable farm. Reduced sunlight has extended crop growth cycles from 30 days to 34 days and reduced his daily yields of leafy greens such as mustard greens, chives and spinach from 16,000kg to 11,000kg over the past few weeks.
He said the particulate matter in the air also made the rain more acidic, triggering fungal infections in his vegetables. The damage is limited for now, but needs close monitoring, he said.
Tan has not yet experienced any revenue loss, but the longer growing cycle is disrupting planting schedules and delaying the next harvest. All this means higher labour costs and less room for profit.
“Haze or no haze, farm work has to go on. We still need to grow and harvest vegetables, sow seeds, apply fertiliser, cut grass and weeds to keep the production cycle going and ensure a steady supply,” he told The Straits Times.
Tourism, aviation worst hit
Sunway University economics professor Yeah Kim Leng told local media that prolonged haze could cost Malaysia RM20 million to RM50 million a day, potentially reaching RM1.5 billion a month if disruptions persist.
“The hardest-hit sectors are tourism and aviation,” he said. “Air pollution can cut arrivals by up to 8%, with gross domestic product losses up to RM1.5 billion.”
In agriculture, he said vegetable farmers in Johor report production declines, fruit yields have halved, and palm oil faces a lagged impact of six months to 12 months.
The haze is also affecting small and medium-sized enterprises.
SME Association of Malaysia president Chin Chee Seong warned that micro and small enterprises are particularly vulnerable because they often operate on thin profit margins and have limited cash reserves.
Even if revenue falls temporarily, businesses must continue paying rent, salaries, utilities, loan instalments and suppliers.
“If the haze continues for weeks, the situation could become more serious, especially for businesses that are already struggling to survive,” Chin told ST.
On social media, small operators have described disruptions. A baker said an event scheduled in Putrajaya, Malaysia’s administrative capital, was cancelled at the last minute, leaving her trying to sell 500 Dubai chewy cookies prepared using 40kg of chocolate and 50kg of strawberries. She had also paid for travel and accommodation expenses.
An operator offering horse therapy classes said sessions had been disrupted for a third consecutive week, while outdoor swimming lessons for kindergarten children were also affected.
Hole in the pocket
Beyond commercial losses, the haze presents a growing healthcare burden. Air quality in several parts of Malaysia remained at unhealthy levels on Oct 16 at 6pm, with the Air Pollutant Index (API), similar to international Air Quality Index (AQI) scales, reaching 160 to 200 in places like Klang in Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
In Seremban, south of Kuala Lumpur, 42-year-old Ahmad Nizam has spent the past week worrying about his four-year-old daughter, who developed a fever, persistent cough and flu-like symptoms that he believes were triggered by the polluted air.
Malaysia’s Health Minister Dzulkefly Ahmad told Parliament on Oct 15 that during a single week in September, upper respiratory tract infections rose 167% to 7,065 cases, asthma surged 127% to 1,117 cases, and conjunctivitis increased 83% to 334 cases. Further increases followed into early October, with haze-related diseases driving up out-of-pocket medical bills for families.
Online, people said frequent clinic visits had cut into their household expenditure, as they reported costs ranging from RM300 for asthma treatments to RM850 for emergency care.
But people and businesses have also been adapting to the haze. Farmer Tan, for instance, has allocated extra land to cultivate price-stable herbs and aromatic plants like curry leaves, turmeric leaves and coriander to help cushion operational overheads.
Economist Barjoyai Bardai emphasised that individual resilience alone is not enough and called for a more systematic approach to measuring the economic costs of the haze by comparing air-quality readings with data on business sales, worker absenteeism, productivity, tourism and agricultural output to establish the true scale of the damage.
“Haze should not be viewed solely as an environmental or public-health issue,” he said. “It is an economic risk that directly affects productivity, household welfare and business resilience.”
Back in Seremban, Ahmad continued to monitor his daughter’s progress and use home remedies to avoid rising medical costs.
“I cannot control the sky, but I will try to keep her safe and healthy,” said Ahmad.

articles.title: Chinese Multinational Corporations and Indonesia’s Quest for Economic Sovereignty - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Chinese Multinational Corporations and Indonesia’s Quest for Economic Sovereignty  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
Foreign investment is often seen as a driver of economic growth. Yet bringing in money does not automatically give a country economic sovereignty. Indonesia’s nickel industry shows this problem: the government has helped build nickel processing, but the industry still depends on Chinese money and technology, raising the question of who really gains from this change.
The United States Geological Survey says Indonesia mined 2.31 million metric tonnes of nickel in 2024, which is about 62 percent of the world’s supply. This makes Indonesia very powerful over a mineral that’s key for stainless steel and some electric vehicle battery technologies.
The main question is whether Indonesia can turn this resource advantage into lasting independence.
Downstreaming: An Economic Opportunity
Indonesia’s nickel downstreaming policy wants to create value inside the country by limiting raw nickel exports and encouraging investment in local processing plants. Of only supplying unprocessed minerals, Indonesia wants to take part more actively in industrial production.
The policy has drawn amounts of money. Indonesia’s Ministry of Investment said that nickel investment reached IDR 153.2 trillion in 2024, adding to a total of IDR 407.8 trillion in the sector.
These numbers show how important downstreaming is to Indonesia’s plan. Chinese multinational firms have helped grow processing capacity by giving money and linking production to established international supply chains.
More production does not automatically mean more domestic control. The International Energy Agency said that even though Indonesia is the nickel miner, Indonesian firms own less than 10 percent of the production, while Chinese firms own about 40 percent. This shows the gap between where resources are mined and who owns the plants that produce them.
Chinese Investment and the Question of Economic Sovereignty
Investment gives Indonesia both chances and problems. It helps expand industry and gives access to money, equipment, and global markets. At the time relying on a small group of investors can limit a country’s ability to diversify its economic ties.
Eve Warburton’s research calls Indonesia’s nickel industry a case of “enclaves”: industry growth driven by national pride but with benefits that are still unevenly shared. The study says that foreign money and linked local businesses have been key to the industry’s growth.
Export patterns also show Indonesia’s trade ties with China. World Bank WITS data says Indonesia sent US$14.06 billion in ferronickel in 2024, and about US$13.26 billion of that went to China. That number is for ferronickel, not all nickel goods, but it shows how big the Chinese market is for this part of Indonesia’s exports.
So the real question is not just whether Chinese investment helps Indonesia. It is whether Indonesia can use that money to build its technology, strengthen local firms, and keep more value from its natural resources.
Balancing Industrial Policy and Global Trade
Indonesia’s downstreaming policy also works inside the trade system. The European Union questioned Indonesia’s nickel export limits at the World Trade Organization. In November 2022 a WTO panel said the export ban and the domestic processing rule do not fit Article XI:1 of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
The dispute shows the tension between Indonesia’s aim to boost its industry and its global trade duties. It also shows that economic sovereignty means more than making rules; governments must follow international rules while chasing domestic growth goals.
For Indonesia the next challenge is to make sure downstreaming gives benefits beyond smelting plants. Technology transfer, local supplier growth, worker training, environmental protection, and more involvement by firms should become key success measures.
Indonesia’s nickel industry shows how a country rich in resources can use policy to boost its spot in global production networks. The rise in nickel production and downstream investment shows the policy has greatly altered Indonesia’s scene. Still, economic sovereignty needs more exports and local processing. It also depends on who owns the assets, who controls technology, and who gets the benefits of industrial growth.
Indonesia does not have to cut its ties with China. Instead, it must make sure that foreign investment builds strength and widens its future economic options.
In the end the success of downstreaming should be judged not by how much nickel Indonesia processes but also by how well the country turns its natural resource strengths into long‑term industrial power and stronger bargaining power in the world economy.

Hanoi (VNA) – Vietnamese brands must become a strategic competitive advantage for the national economy, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung said on October 16, urging businesses to shift from cost-based advantages to value creation, innovation and stronger participation in global value chains. 
The PM made the statement at a ceremony in Hanoi announcing products awarded the Vietnam National Brand title in 2026. The event was organised by the Vietnam National Brand Council and the Ministry of Industry and Trade. 
This year, 499 products from 227 businesses were recognised across a range of sectors, including processing – manufacturing, agriculture and food, pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, finance and banking, telecommunications and technology, transport and logistics, and trade and services. 
Over more than two decades, the Vietnam National Brand (Vietnam Value) programme has helped establish common standards for businesses, linking brand value not only to recognition or communication but also to product quality, governance capacity, technology, innovation, market responsiveness and social responsibility. 
The number of businesses with recognised products has risen more than sevenfold, from 30 in 2008 to 227 this year. Fourteen businesses have retained the title in all 10 selection rounds, while 84 have received it at least five times. 
In 2026, Vietnam’s nation brand value reached 462.279 billion USD in 2026, up 45.14% from 2020, ranking 32nd among 193 countries. 
Five businesses with nationally branded products are among the country’s 10 most valuable brands this year, accounting for about 69.1% of the group’s total value. 
The 2026 selection process also introduced revised criteria, giving greater weight to innovation, research and development, science – technology application, intellectual property, digital transformation, green growth and workforce development. Innovation accounted for 30% of the total score. 
Congratulating the honoured businesses, PM Hung said the recognition reflects their resilience, wisdom, creativity and sustained efforts, as well as the contributions of Vietnamese businesses, entrepreneurs and workers.
He stressed that the National Brand title is not only a source of pride but also an honourable commitment to consumers and a responsibility towards the country’s reputation. Every Vietnamese-branded product should strongly demonstrate quality, credibility and the ambition to compete internationally. 
He noted that a brand is not merely an asset belonging to an individual enterprise; it also represents a nation’s competitiveness, reputation, and standing. Strong brands constitute strong enterprises, and robust enterprises, in turn, contribute to the autonomy and resilience of the national economy, ultimately fostering a powerful and prosperous nation. 
PM Hung said Vietnam is entering a new development phase, with a target of average annual GDP growth of at least 10% during 2026–2030. Achieving this requires strong development model reform, as well as improvements in economic capacity, quality and competitiveness, driven by science, technology, innovation and digital transformation. 
He cited economic results in the first nine months of 2026, when GDP grew 9.01% year on year, with third-quarter growth reaching 9.95%. Vietnam’s total import-export turnover is estimated to reach 1.1 trillion USD for the year, surpassing 1 trillion USD for the first time. The country ranked 43rd out of 139 economies in the 2026 Global Innovation Index and led the world in the shares of high-tech and creative goods exports in total merchandise trade. 
These achievements, he said, reflect direct and important contributions by businesses, particularly those leading in quality, technology and brand development. 
However, the PM noted that many good products still lack strong brands, while domestic value added and market control remain limited. Exports by businesses with nationally branded products accounted for only about 11% of their own total revenue, equivalent to around 2.3% of Vietnam’s overall export turnover. Investment in research, core technologies, intellectual property protection and the fight against counterfeit goods also needs to improve. 
The Government leader referred to the Party’s strategic resolutions, including targets for more private businesses to join global value chains and for stronger state-owned enterprises to compete internationally. Vietnam, he said, must move from cost advantages to value creation, from processing and assembly to design and innovation, and from market participation to a leading position. 
The PM called on businesses, especially those with nationally branded products, to take the lead in implementing the Party’s strategic policies, raising productivity, increasing domestic value added, expanding market share and joining global value chains more deeply. 
He also urged leading businesses to treat their brands as long-term strategic assets and set examples in product quality, corporate governance and social responsibility, helping strengthen the reputation and competitiveness of Vietnamese brands worldwide./.

Happy Friday. Stocks were mixed Friday as Wall Street looked to recover from another tech sell-off.

"US and Asian equities have borne the brunt of the sell-off, after hotter US CPI pushed Treasury yields higher and renewed concerns about the financing behind the AI boom."
Hathorn said the Nasdaq has been particularly vulnerable as investors question whether future AI returns can justify both elevated valuations and increasingly expensive borrowing costs.
Shares of cloud-computing provider CoreWeave (CRWV) were down 4.15% in premarket trading.

CoreWeave's slump fueled a global rout in AI stocks, underscoring investor doubts about whether future revenue from the technology can keep pace with the spending.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is CoreWeave's second-largest investor with about a 10% stake, played down the fears.
"CoreWeave's financial strength is improving every day," Huang told reporters at a Stockholm event, adding that he does not see a need for Nvidia to backstop the company. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."
Hathorn said Huang's comments may have reduced the sense of immediate crisis, "but upcoming Big Tech earnings will still need to demonstrate that the enormous investment in AI is translating into sufficient revenue and cash flow to justify the cost."

articles.title: Ho Chi Minh City, a "megacity": Infrastructure paves the way, governance creates momentum. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Ho Chi Minh City, a "megacity": Infrastructure paves the way, governance creates momentum.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
New space - new opportunities
 With its vast development potential after the merger, Ho Chi Minh City is facing the opportunity to restructure its economy , reorganize its urban system, and create new growth drivers. Ho Chi Minh City has the conditions to connect financial, commercial, industrial, logistics, port, and tourism centers within a unified development space. This presents an opportunity to form new economic linkages, instead of developing relatively independent areas as before.
 However, a larger scale also means higher demands on planning, infrastructure connectivity, resource mobilization, and governance capacity.
 At the seminar "Investing in Synchronized Infrastructure Development – A Driving Force for Economic Growth and Expanding the Development Space of Ho Chi Minh City," Deputy Minister of Construction Nguyen Tuong Van emphasized the requirement for urban development based on a multi-polar, multi-center model, linking spatial planning with transportation systems, housing, and economic activities. According to this orientation, modern urban development is not simply about expanding construction area or creating new urban areas on the map. 
 Deputy Minister of Construction Nguyen Tuong Van. Photo: Duy Quang
 "The new space facilitates the connection of financial, commercial, and service centers with industrial and innovation centers, seaports, logistics, marine economy, and unique ecological zones. This is a historic opportunity for the city to restructure its growth model, but at the same time, it places very high demands on planning, infrastructure investment, and implementation capacity," Deputy Minister Nguyen Tuong Van commented.
 One of the key tasks is to reorganize the development space, ensuring that growth poles are interconnected and mutually supportive. Infrastructure systems must play a leading role, rather than merely responding to emerging needs once the city has formed.
 From an implementation perspective, the Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Department of Construction, Tran Quang Lam, stated that the city is focusing on developing strategic transportation projects, including ring roads, expressways, urban railways, and connecting routes to important transportation hubs.
 The goal by 2030 is to gradually complete the main transportation network, strengthening connectivity between areas within the new urban space. Simultaneously, tasks include urban beautification, canal renovation, and improving the quality of infrastructure serving the people.
 From the request mechanism to the capacity for creation.
 In a private interview with VTV Times on the sidelines of the conference, Associate Professor Tran Dinh Thien stated that the most fundamental issue for Ho Chi Minh City to realize its potential as a megacity is removing institutional bottlenecks. According to him, granting the city more autonomy is a necessary direction. "However, authority must be coupled with responsibility and, especially, the capacity to implement," he said.
 The Urban Development Law of 2026, effective from October 1st, is seen by Mr. Thien as a crucial opportunity for the city to shift to a more proactive development approach. Under the previous management mechanism, localities typically operated within established frameworks; any additional resources or special mechanisms required proposals and permission. With greater autonomy, the government cannot simply continue to perform pre-existing tasks. Instead, it is required to identify problems, proactively seek solutions, organize implementation, and take responsibility for the results.
 According to Associate Professor Tran Dinh Thien, this represents a fundamental shift in the capacity of the administrative apparatus: "From being accustomed to the role of execution, to a creative and proactive mindset. Having the power to make decisions is important, but more importantly, having the capacity to effectively utilize that power is crucial."
 He also noted that long-term development planning requires the ability to recognize global changes. Changes in trade, technology, geoeconomics, and international capital flows can quickly create new opportunities while altering the advantages of each region. Therefore, governance capacity lies not only in building and implementing plans, but also in the ability to forecast, adapt, and adjust strategies in the face of unprecedented situations.
 Notably, Mr. Thien distinguished between two groups of capabilities that Ho Chi Minh City needs to develop: physical capabilities and institutional capabilities. While physical capabilities are reflected in infrastructure, capital resources, and conditions serving production and business, institutional capabilities create an environment where those resources can be mobilized and used effectively. 
 Architect Ngo Viet Nam Son (left) and Assoc. Prof. Dr. Tran Dinh Thien. Photo: The Ha
 Urban development capacity is more important than mega-projects.
 If institutional capacity determines the ability to pave the way for development, then planning and coordination capacity will determine how those opportunities are realized. Architect Ngo Viet Nam Son argues that in a megacity, the development of key infrastructure must be linked to the socio-economic development program of each area. It is unacceptable to only implement individual transportation projects or real estate projects without a comprehensive connection.
 Taking the two banks of the Saigon River as an example, Mr. Son commented that the planning of the existing central area and Thu Thiem has its own strengths, but the relatively independent planning process has meant that the strategic connection has not been fully realized.
 According to him, the two riverbanks should be approached as a closely interconnected urban space, thereby better exploiting the value of infrastructure and investment opportunities.
 For Thu Thiem, the goal is not just to build a modern new urban center. More importantly, it's to create a community with conditions for living, working, employment, schools, hospitals, parks, and essential amenities. This requires coordination among various sectors and levels of government, as well as the participation of businesses and residents. Real estate projects, transportation infrastructure, and social infrastructure must be organized within a unified development program.
 Another noteworthy issue raised by architect Ngo Viet Nam Son is how to leverage land value from public transportation systems. According to him, developing urban railways and transport-oriented development (TOD) areas will increase real estate values, creating opportunities to attract investment. However, if house and land prices around metro lines rise too high, those who need to use public transportation may not be able to afford to live there.
 At that time, one of the key objectives of TOD—bringing people closer to public transportation—would be difficult to achieve. Therefore, the city needs to carefully consider land allocation for affordable housing and workspaces, while also ensuring the availability of schools, hospitals, parks, and essential services. This problem demonstrates that urban governance capacity is not just about attracting investment or implementing projects. More importantly, it's about the ability to harmonize interests and ensure infrastructure development creates value for both the economy and the community.
 From the institutional perspective of Associate Professor Tran Dinh Thien to the planning approach of architect Ngo Viet Nam Son, it is clear that the demands placed on Ho Chi Minh City go beyond simply expanding space or accelerating investment. A megacity needs the capacity for self-determination, policy innovation, multi-sectoral coordination, resource mobilization, and effective implementation. The strength of such a megacity is not measured solely by its area, population, or multi-billion dollar projects. It also lies in its ability to transform resources into growth, transform growth into improved quality of life for its citizens, and turn opportunities into long-term development achievements.

articles.full_text:
Household deposits at banks at the end of August reached over 11.43 million billion VND, an increase of 10.6% compared to the beginning of the year, reflecting a positive flow of money in the economy.
According to data from the State Bank of Vietnam, by the end of August, household deposits in the banking system reached over 11.43 million billion VND. This figure is nearly 1.1 million billion VND higher, equivalent to a 10.6% increase, compared to the beginning of the year.
In August alone, household deposits increased net by nearly 214,000 billion VND compared to the end of July, averaging an increase of about 6,900 billion VND per day.
This is the second largest monthly increase since the beginning of the year, after June 2026 (an increase of approximately VND 445 trillion, equivalent to 2.62%) and significantly higher than the almost flat increase in July (an increase of only nearly VND 21 trillion, equivalent to 0.12%).
The flow of household funds into the banking system has tended to strengthen since the second quarter of this year. In the last five months, household deposits have increased net by an average of 175,000 billion VND per month, nearly 2.4 times higher than the average of the preceding five months.
Since the end of April, the highest listed interest rates in the system (excluding large deposits or VIP customers) have sharply increased to 7.6%-7.8% per year. The actual preferential interest rates at many banks range from 8.5% to 9.5% per year without requiring a minimum deposit, or only around 100-200 million VND.
You may also like
Bank leaders all agree that the interest rate differential between Vietnamese dong and foreign currencies is attractive, making individual customers increasingly prefer holding Vietnamese dong. Intense competition to attract deposits has led banks to continuously launch new deposit products and incentives to attract customers.
Developments since the beginning of the year show that corporate deposits have been volatile, decreasing in January and February (the peak payment period around Tet), increasing sharply in the last months of the quarter such as March and June, and then decreasing again in the first month of the next quarter.
In the first eight months of the year, deposits from economic organizations increased by only nearly 157,000 billion VND, equivalent to 2.54%, much lower than the growth rate of the household sector.
In total, deposits from individuals and economic organizations in the banking system reached over 17.77 million billion VND at the end of August, an increase of approximately 1.26 million billion VND, equivalent to 7.6%, compared to the beginning of the year.
While deposit growth has been positive, it has not kept pace with the rate of capital injection into the economy. According to data released by the State Bank of Vietnam at its Q3 press conference on October 7th, total outstanding credit in the banking system reached approximately VND 20.75 trillion by September 30th, 2026, an increase of 11.59% compared to the end of 2025. This has kept the competition for capital mobilization among banks high in recent months.

articles.summary: Nearly $5.4 billion is about to flow into the pockets of banks.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to the latest report on the banking sector from SSI Securities Company's Analysis Center (SSI Research), experts say that capital raising is becoming an inevitable trend for banks in the new era.
 Accordingly, GDP growth is expected to be sustained in the medium term, thanks to stable FDI inflows and an ambitious public infrastructure investment portfolio, with a target of average growth of around 10% during the 2026-2030 period.
 In a context where the capital market still needs many years to absorb long-term risks, banks remain the primary source of funding, financing projects throughout the construction phase before refinancing them for long-term investors. Consequently, pressure on balance sheets has led an increasing number of banks to raise additional equity and debt capital to sustain credit growth.
 Eight banks plan to raise nearly $5.4 billion .
 According to the research unit, eight banks have announced plans to issue shares with a total value of approximately VND 144,000 billion (approximately USD 5.4 billion ), of which NCB Bank, Vietcombank, and BIDV account for nearly two-thirds of the total value.
 Most large banks issued less than 15% of their outstanding shares, while smaller banks such as NCB (113%), PVcomBank (33%), and MSB (25%) pursued more aggressive capital increase plans to strengthen their capital buffers. 
|  | 
|  Eight banks have planned to raise capital. | 
 Overall, the new capital will help increase the equity of listed banks by approximately 6.9%, along with additional support from retained earnings in 2027.
 However, analysts believe that this additional capital is still insufficient to meet investment needs in the coming years. The period from 2026 to 2030 requires a significantly faster increase in total investment capital compared to recent trends. While the state budget is expected to meet only about one-fifth of the needs, the private sector will have to bear the majority of the increased capital requirements, and much of this capital still depends on bank credit.
 In the short term, switching to an Internal Rating Based (IRB) methodology is estimated to help raise reported capital adequacy ratios (CAR) by 1.5-2%, giving banks more time before being forced to increase capital.
 However, SSI Research notes that this improvement needs to be viewed cautiously. Accordingly, historical data showing a near-zero default rate among real estate developers may not fully reflect the risks, as troubled loans are often restructured rather than definitively resolved.
 Given the focus of credit on this customer group, the reported CAR likely reflects a higher actual loss-absorbing capacity if the owners' cycles... Real estate investment trends reverse.
 Therefore, capital raising will be a recurring theme in the coming years, especially for banks aiming for higher-than-average growth rates compared to the system.
 With increased credit, banks face additional capital pressure.
 Also in this report, SSI Research forecasts that credit across the entire system will increase by approximately 16-17% in 2027. Specifically, the group of banks under its monitoring is expected to grow by 17.9%, led by MB, VPBank, and HDBank – banks that received the mandatory transfer of weak credit institutions.
 The credit lines are expected to focus on the construction, infrastructure, and related sectors, in line with the trend of boosting public investment, upgrading infrastructure, and developing logistics networks connecting key economic centers.
 SSI forecasts that achieving high credit growth to support the ambitious double-digit GDP growth target could put continued pressure on banks' capital resources.
 In the short term, SSI Research believes that time deposits will continue to be the main source of funding for banks, and expects the issuance of certificates of deposit and bonds to accelerate next year in order to narrow the credit-deposit gap.
 Public investment is the second but slower-paced supporting driver, and foreign loans are only a supplementary source. SSI Research believes that the disbursement rate in 2027 may slow down as projects move into the construction phase, while USD-denominated loans are limited by the costs of hedging against exchange rate and inflation risks. 
|  | 
|  Vietnamese banks' plans for borrowing foreign capital in 2026. | 
 The three channels mentioned above help reduce short-term pressure, while the sustainable solution is to shift long-term risks off the bank's balance sheet.
 According to SSI Research, Vietnam's credit-to-GDP ratio has reached 140-150%, while the portfolio of announced mega-projects alone could absorb at least 30% of the net credit increase during the 2026-2030 period, and likely even more.
 There are two approaches that could help alleviate this pressure. In the public sector, the government could provide more direct funding for infrastructure through concessional loans guaranteed by the government , project bonds, PPP bonds, and local government bonds that can finance the construction phase from the outset.
 In the private sector, the public sector's first-loss guarantee mechanism can support businesses, making bonds issued by investors attractive enough to attract capital from this sector.
 However, in the baseline scenario, SSI believes that no solution will bring about significant change in 2027. Therefore, banks will still be both initiators and holders of infrastructure risks, and recent easing measures will only delay, not resolve, the capital shortage.
 Pressure on banks
 Regarding banks' Net Interest Margin (NIM), SSI forecasts a slight decrease of 2 basis points to 3.11% across the entire sector in 2027. However, this overall figure does not fully reflect the increasing divergence: the NIM of state-owned commercial banks is projected to increase by 2 basis points, while that of private joint-stock commercial banks is expected to decrease by 8 basis points.
 This difference stems from the capital structure.
 While state-owned commercial banks, with their deposit base from large enterprises and FDI, possess a lower-cost and more stable source of CASA (current account deposits), mitigating the impact of a high interest rate environment, private commercial banks lack this buffer. Banks with large credit limits (MB, VPBank , HDBank) maintain high deposit interest rates to finance growth, while smaller banks must pay high interest rates to retain their customer base.
 The difference in 2027 is that lending activity also puts pressure on net interest margins. As credit skewed towards infrastructure, banks have to hold assets with low profit margins and long maturities but financed by high-cost short-term capital – this is a structural rather than cyclical pressure.
 For private banks, this makes the trade-off between protecting net interest margin (NIM) through higher-yield loans and maintaining asset quality more difficult. This is also the challenge that will shape the year 2027 for these banks.
 While net interest income is under pressure, experts at SSI expect banks' service fee segments to experience outstanding growth, driven by guarantees, trade finance, and standby letters of credit (L/C).
 The asset quality of banks is also projected to continue deteriorating in 2027, particularly among private banks. Prolonged high interest rates could impact the debt repayment capacity of SMEs, household businesses, and homebuyers. Further pressure comes from over 100 trillion VND in maturing corporate bonds.
 SSI estimates that outstanding loans to real estate developers across the entire banking system have reached approximately VND 2.5 trillion , equivalent to 48% of total real estate loans and about VND 1.4 trillion higher than in 2023. This scale means that the quality of banks' assets depends heavily on the repayment capacity of developers in the context of high capital costs.

articles.title: US inflation returns: Vietnam responds to unpredictable variables. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: US inflation returns: Vietnam responds to unpredictable variables.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Rising US inflation could put pressure on Vietnam's exchange rate and import and export costs, at a time when the economy is aiming for double-digit growth. Given these unpredictable external fluctuations, the key is to manage policies flexibly, maintain macroeconomic stability, and strengthen domestic capabilities to enhance the economy's resilience.
According to data released on October 14th by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the consumer price index (CPI) for September 2026 increased by 3.7% year-on-year, higher than the 3.4% in August; core inflation rose from 2.4% to 2.6%. Prior to this, the Federal Reserve (Fed) raised its policy interest rate by 0.25 percentage points in September, to 3.75-4%. This development increases the likelihood that the Fed will maintain its tight monetary policy for longer than expected.
For Vietnam, the impact could be transmitted through three main channels: monetary policy and exchange rates; commodity prices and import costs; and consumer demand and imports in the US market. While GDP in the first nine months of 2026 increased by 9.01% and the average CPI increased by 4.52%, the economy must both maintain growth momentum and control price pressures.
First, if US inflation continues to rise, the Fed may keep interest rates high, making USD-denominated assets more attractive and encouraging international capital flows back to the US. This could put pressure on exchange rates in emerging economies, including Vietnam. The State Bank of Vietnam must therefore balance exchange rate stability, inflation control, and ensuring funding for production and business activities.
However, it cannot be assumed that rising US inflation will automatically lead to an appreciation of the USD. The exchange rate also depends on market expectations, interest rate differentials, growth prospects, and the policies of other economies. In fact, the USD price index in Vietnam in September 2026 decreased by 0.69% compared to the previous month. Therefore, monetary policy management needs to closely monitor actual developments and avoid a mechanical reaction to a single indicator.
The second impact channel is import costs. In the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam imported $453.72 billion worth of goods, an increase of 36.7% compared to the same period; production materials accounted for 94.1% of the total import value. Of this, machinery, equipment, tools and spare parts accounted for 58.3%; raw materials, fuels and other materials accounted for 35.8%.
This structure shows that domestic production remains significantly dependent on imported inputs. When the exchange rate rises, the prices of raw materials, components, and equipment converted to Vietnamese Dong can increase even if the prices in USD remain unchanged. The electronics, mechanical engineering, chemical, plastics, textile, and equipment manufacturing industries are at risk of facing significant pressure. Rising fuel prices also lead to increased transportation and logistics costs, further increasing the prices of goods and services.
It is necessary to distinguish the impact of exchange rates from fluctuations in international commodity prices. Rising energy prices may simultaneously push inflation higher in both the US and Vietnam, but this is a general shock to the global market, not simply a ripple effect from US inflation. Identifying the correct cause is fundamental to choosing appropriate policy tools.
The third channel is trade. Prolonged inflation could erode the purchasing power of American consumers, while high interest rates put pressure on consumption and investment. In the first nine months of 2026, Vietnam's goods exports to the US reached approximately $140 billion, accounting for 32.2% of the country's total export turnover. If US import demand slows down, orders, industrial production, and jobs in Vietnam could be affected.
However, a decline in real wages does not necessarily mean an immediate weakening of overall consumer demand. Real consumer spending in the US in August still increased by 0.6% compared to the previous month. Therefore, it is necessary to monitor real income, purchasing power, import orders, and interest rate developments simultaneously to accurately assess the level of risk.
The most worrying aspect is not the one-month increase in US inflation, but rather the scenario of prolonged high inflation leading the Fed to maintain high interest rates while US economic growth weakens. In that case, Vietnam could simultaneously face rising input costs, slowing exports, and shrinking policy space to support growth.
Coordinate policies and preserve room for growth.
Given that GDP grew by 9.01% in the first nine months, the average CPI increased by 4.52%, and core inflation increased by 4.26%, achieving a growth target of 10% or more while keeping average inflation around 4.5% poses a significant challenge. This requires close coordination between monetary and fiscal policies, rather than placing too much burden on a single instrument.
You may also like
Regarding monetary policy, the priority is maintaining macroeconomic stability while ensuring sufficient capital for efficient production and business activities. Exchange rates need to be managed flexibly to absorb some external shocks, limiting excessive fluctuations that could disrupt inflation expectations and maintain financial stability. Interest rate, liquidity, and foreign exchange intervention tools should be coordinated based on actual market developments.
In particular, credit expansion should not be accelerated solely to stimulate short-term growth. Capital should be prioritized for businesses with viable business plans, strong orders, and good repayment capacity; while controlling sectors with potential financial imbalances. The efficiency of capital utilization should be given more importance than mere credit growth.
With limited room for monetary easing, fiscal policy needs to play a more prominent role in supporting growth. The focus should be on accelerating the disbursement of public investment, especially in transportation, energy, and logistics infrastructure projects that can reduce production costs, improve connectivity, and expand supply capacity.
By the end of September 2026, disbursed public investment capital reached approximately VND 642.96 trillion, equivalent to 62.9% of the plan assigned by the Prime Minister . To accelerate progress in the remaining months of the year, it is necessary to focus on removing obstacles related to procedures, land clearance, materials, and organizational responsibilities. However, disbursement must be linked to the quality and efficiency of investment, avoiding chasing deadlines at all costs.
In addition, targeted and time-limited tax and fee support could be considered for industries heavily impacted by energy prices and input costs. The policy needs to clearly identify beneficiaries, assess effectiveness, and ensure budget balance, avoiding widespread support.
An important principle is to distinguish between demand-pull inflation and cost-push inflation. If domestic aggregate demand increases too rapidly, monetary policy plays a crucial role in controlling demand. But if price pressures mainly come from energy, transportation, and imported raw materials, excessive monetary tightening can weaken production without addressing the underlying causes.
In this case, priority should be given to ensuring the supply of essential goods, reducing logistics costs, improving the distribution system, and providing targeted support to severely affected groups. Price stabilization policies also need to be cautious, avoiding prolonged administrative interventions that distort market signals.
For businesses, it is necessary to improve their capacity to manage exchange rate and cash flow risks. Businesses that borrow in USD but have their main revenue sources in Vietnamese Dong will face pressure when the exchange rate increases; while export businesses with foreign currency revenue may benefit from converting it to Vietnamese Dong. The extent of the impact depends on the proportion of imported raw materials, foreign currency payment obligations, and the ability to negotiate selling prices.
Therefore, it is necessary to develop tools for hedging against exchange rate risks, increase access to financial information and advice, and help businesses proactively balance their foreign currency revenues and expenditures. Working capital support should focus on businesses that are efficient in production and trading, capable of maintaining orders and repaying debts.
Enhancing the self-reliance of the economy.
Fluctuations in the US economy demonstrate that macroeconomic stability cannot rely solely on short-term response measures. In the long term, Vietnam's resilience depends on its ability to reduce vulnerabilities in its production structure, exports, and input supply.
First and foremost, it is necessary to diversify export markets, supply partners, and raw material sources. Expanding into the EU, Japan , and other potential markets will help reduce over-reliance on a single market. Diversification does not mean diminishing the role of the US, but rather creating alternative options when demand in one market fluctuates.
Simultaneously, it is necessary to improve the quality and added value of exports. In the first nine months of 2026, the foreign-invested enterprise sector accounted for 80.7% of total merchandise exports. This proportion demonstrates the important role of the FDI sector and simultaneously highlights the need to enhance the participation capacity of domestic enterprises in higher value-added stages.

articles.title: Lesson 4: Opening up capital flows for projects with a ripple effect. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Lesson 4: Opening up capital flows for projects with a ripple effect.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Machinery and manpower are being mobilized to the maximum extent to construct the various components along the entire route of the Tran Hung Dao bridge ( Hanoi ). Photo: Vu Quang/TTXVN
 To achieve double-digit economic growth, large-scale infrastructure, urban development, energy, industrial projects, and new growth drivers require enormous capital. However, with bank credit remaining the primary source of funding, the challenge is not simply "injecting more capital," but rather opening up the right opportunities for projects with significant spillover effects, while maintaining credit discipline and risk control.
 From the capital city's funding problem
 According to a report by the Hanoi People's Committee, the total projected public investment capital for the period 2026-2030 is approximately 865,000 billion VND, while the capital that can be proactively balanced only meets less than 41% of the need. The remainder must be mobilized from bank credit, capital markets, ODA, and private capital through public-private partnerships (PPP).
 As of June 30, 2026, 13 credit institutions had participated in financing 29 major and important programs and projects in Hanoi, with a total committed credit amount of over 63,000 billion VND, but the outstanding loan balance was only nearly 15,000 billion VND. The gap between commitment and disbursement shows that capital flow into projects is not guaranteed just because a bank is ready to provide it.
 According to Ms. Nguyen Thi Hoa , Director of the State Bank of Vietnam Region 1, major and important programs and projects in Hanoi have large capital scales, long implementation and payback periods, and require concentrated disbursement in each stage. Therefore, it is necessary to mobilize many resources simultaneously with appropriate financing structures and methods.
 Even the banks' capacity to supply capital is limited. In the first eight months of 2026, credit in Hanoi increased by 13.05%, while deposits increased by 10.78%. The higher growth rate of credit than deposits puts pressure on costs and capital balance, especially as the peak disbursement period for important projects is expected to be concentrated in 2027-2029.
 In addition, there are "bottlenecks" outside the banking sector, including: planning, investment procedures, land allocation, site clearance, financial obligations, and project progress. When legal documents are incomplete, credit institutions, even with readily available capital, cannot disburse funds.
 This is a challenge not only for Hanoi, but also for large projects nationwide. Accordingly, capital needs must be in sync with the ability to mobilize and absorb capital, so that money is injected into the economy at the right time and effectively.
 More room for maneuver, but no lowering of standards.
 Economist Dr. Nguyen Minh Phong believes that the previous credit classification method could have resulted in many loans of very different natures being counted as real estate credit. The new mechanism issued by the State Bank of Vietnam, which allows separating policy-oriented, safe, and necessary credit for growth, such as social housing or key projects, from banks' credit growth limits, is "quite reasonable."
 According to expert analysis, if capital allocated to key projects is also included in a single real estate credit framework, banks may have limited room for lending to other production and business activities. In that case, the very projects that are supposed to drive growth could become factors that reduce the supply of capital to other sectors of the economy.
 This is also the direction set by the State Bank of Vietnam in its operational guidance. Governor Pham Duc An stated that the regulatory body has implemented solutions to exclude some newly arising loan balances and to grant additional credit growth limits to commercial banks for lending to businesses implementing large-scale, key projects with spillover effects and linkages, promoting regional and local economic development to achieve the "double-digit" growth target.
 However, expanding credit availability does not mean loosening lending standards. Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Duc An, emphasized that credit growth must go hand in hand with the ability to mobilize capital and the economy's absorption capacity; banks need to create conditions for businesses to access capital at reasonable costs but "without lowering credit standards." The State Bank also requested that credit be directed towards key projects and works with full legal compliance, efficiency, and repayment capacity; and that co-financing, syndicated loans, and the application of data and technology in appraisal and risk management be strengthened.
 This is a crucial boundary in credit policy during the growth-promoting phase, which may change how lending capacity is allocated, but cannot lower the standards for loan quality.
 Dr. Nguyen Minh Phong also raised the issue of risk management very early on: “For large projects, banks need to closely monitor the investor and management agencies, only disburse funds according to cash flow and project progress, not in a lump sum; at the same time, they require transparency of information, regular reporting, continuous inspection and review, and the development of risk response scenarios.”
 From "lending" to capital structures for growth.
 A larger problem is that bank credit alone cannot finance the entire long-term capital needs of the economy.
 Governor Pham Duc An emphasized: "Bank credit cannot and should not be the sole source of funding for all development needs." For large-scale projects with long lifecycles, a combination of equity capital, bank credit, public investment, PPPs, capital markets, ODA, and other legitimate resources is necessary to increase sustainability and reduce maturity pressure on the banking system.
 From a banking perspective, Mr. Nguyen Thien Hoang, Deputy General Director of the Vietnam Investment and Development Bank ( BIDV ), stated that the bank is ready to act as a lead in arranging capital, syndicated loans domestically and internationally, and connect member companies in the securities, insurance, and leasing sectors to provide comprehensive financial solutions. This approach also demonstrates that the bank's role is shifting from simply "lending" to participating in designing and arranging the financial structure for large projects.
 Meanwhile, Mr. Bach Thanh Long, Deputy General Director of Vietnam Foreign Trade Commercial Bank ( Vietcombank ), emphasized the role of the capital market when proposing to increase the attractiveness of Hanoi Capital Bonds. The demand for fundraising through this channel in the 2027-2030 period is expected to be around 150,000-200,000 billion VND, but to maximize effectiveness, it is necessary to improve secondary market liquidity, diversify maturities and denominations, and expand the investor base.
 The perspective from Hanoi is also a microcosm of the economy. Achieving double-digit growth requires a massive amount of capital deployed simultaneously across multiple sectors. While the banking system plays a pivotal role, placing all the pressure on the balance sheets and maturities of banks carries significant risks. Therefore, it is necessary to combine multiple fundraising channels simultaneously, such as public investment, PPPs, capital markets, ODA, and private capital.
 To unlock these resources, the decisive factor lies in the quality of the project. According to the State Bank of Vietnam, a project with transparent legal status, a clear schedule, and a feasible financial plan will help credit institutions accurately assess the project, thereby making disbursement decisions more quickly and safely.
 Therefore, untangling the credit bottleneck does not mean loosening lending at all costs. The challenge is to open up the right space, allocate capital to the right areas, tightly manage cash flow, and maximize non-bank resources. That is the only way for credit to become a lever to promote projects with widespread impact, instead of increasing risks to the system's safety. In the race for breakthrough growth, what the economy needs is not just more capital, but a more optimal capital structure and a more efficient allocation mechanism.

articles.title: Palm Oil Rallies on Supply Concerns, Eyes Second Weekly Gain - TradingView
articles.summary: Palm Oil Rallies on Supply Concerns, Eyes Second Weekly Gain  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Malaysian palm oil futures surged more than 3% to above MYR 4,750 per tonne, erasing prior losses and hitting a three-week high.
Firmer edible oils on China’s Dalian exchange and Chicago markets boosted sentiment, while supply concerns in top producer Indonesia also added support.
The Indonesian Palm Oil Association projected output to fall to 51.7 million tonnes in 2027 from 53.7 million this year, with exports seen dropping nearly 15% yoy amid rising domestic biodiesel and food consumption.
Meanwhile, cargo surveyors reported Malaysian shipments jumping 33.5%–37.7% in October 1–10 from the same period in September, signaling stronger near-term demand.
Robust festival buying from India, the world's largest palm oil importer, further buoyed prices.
However, record-high Malaysian inventories and growing caution ahead of Q3 GDP data next week in China, a major palm oil consumer, tempered gains.
For the week, futures were on track for a second straight advance, up about 3.9% so far.

articles.title: From niche to mainstream - Vietnam Economic Times
articles.summary: From niche to mainstream  Vietnam Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Born in the “Roaring 20s” with the launch of the Sherry-Netherland Hotel on Fifth Avenue in New York City, branded residences are properties where the developer partners with a well-known brand to create a guarantee of quality and the promise of an exceptional living experience. A surge in popularity since the turn of the millennium has pushed branded residences to the forefront of the real estate market for high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs). The concept continues to gain traction around Asia.
According to the Branded Residences 2026 Report from Savills, released in September, the Asia-Pacific is currently the second-most established branded residential region globally, accounting for approximately 23 per cent of all completed schemes worldwide. While the region continues to demonstrate impressive momentum, with a further 187 projects expected to be delivered by 2032, the nature of its growth story is evolving.
As Vietnam’s property sector proved increasingly favorable among international investors due to its stellar economic growth, global hoteliers have accelerated their push into the country’s branded residence segment. Savills reported that Vietnam currently leads the Top 10 countries in the region in the number of branded residence projects, with supply forecast to increase by 152 per cent by 2032.
New entrants
In early September, IHG Hotels & Resorts and the Alphanam Group announced their collaboration on The Residences at InterContinental Sapa Resort, marking the debut of InterContinental branded residences in Vietnam’s northwest region. Located in the spectacular Muong Hoa Valley in Sapa, Lao Cai province, the development represents a significant milestone for IHG’s luxury residential portfolio in one of Vietnam’s most culturally-rich and naturally-distinctive destinations.
The residences will form part of the 83-ha Alphora Muong Hoa International Resort Complex, developed by the Alphanam Group. The Residences at InterContinental Sapa Resort will comprise 79 branded villas, offering homeowners access to range of hotel facilities and services, including dining, wellness, concierge, and hospitality experiences.
“This landmark development brings together the global strength and legacy of the InterContinental brand with the distinctive character and natural beauty of Muong Hoa Valley, creating an exceptional branded residential offering in one of Vietnam’s most remarkable destinations,” said Mr. Bryan Chan, Vice President, Development, Southeast Asia & Korea, at IHG Hotels & Resorts. “As Vietnam continues to growth its position as one of the world’s leading branded residences markets, this project reflects the increasing demand for high-quality branded living experiences and our long-term confidence in the country’s hospitality and residential sectors.”
The launch further expands IHG’s luxury and lifestyle presence in Vietnam and reinforces the company’s strategy of growing its branded residences portfolio in high-potential destinations across the region. IHG currently has 35 branded residential projects open or in the sales phases with the owner or developer, across 19 countries, with additional opportunities in the pipeline. Signings in 2026 to date for future branded residences developments included The Regent Ho Tram in Vietnam.
Previously, in February, Marriott International announced a milestone agreement with Masterise Group to develop a branded residential project in Vietnam. The launch of The Ritz-Carlton, Saigon and The Ritz-Carlton Residences, Saigon is poised to set a new benchmark for luxury hospitality in Vietnam.
“Our collaboration with Masterise Group is founded on a shared vision and a long-term commitment to excellence,” said Mr. Gautam Bhandari, Chief Development Officer, Asia Pacific excluding China at Marriott International. “Together, we are developing projects that we expect to stand as enduring icons and operated in full alignment with the rigorous quality standards of Marriott International’s world-leading brands.”
Last year, JW Marriott Residences, Grand Marina Saigon, Sea, opened its doors in Ho Chi Minh City’s District 1, marking the debut of the brand’s first urban branded residence in the Asia-Pacific. Standing 47 floors high, Sea Tower is positioned to provide uninterrupted panoramic views of the Saigon River, setting a new standard for branded luxury living in Vietnam.
Marriott International also signed another agreement with Masterise Group to bring Hanoi at The Grand, the Ritz-Carlton Residences to life with the promise of delivering to Vietnam the ideal structure of branded residences with benchmarked Ritz-Carlton’s global standards and luxury offerings in the market.
Next growth hotspot
Across the Asia-Pacific, according to the Savills report, the share of standalone branded residence projects is forecast to decline from 30 per cent of completed supply to 16 per cent of the future pipeline, as the integrated residential-hotel model becomes increasingly common. Meanwhile, in Ho Chi Minh City and Bangkok, Thailand, the number of standalone projects in the pipeline expected to be developed through 2032 is projected to double.
This trend shows that the potential for branded residences in Vietnam is expanding across multiple models, from destination resort products to branded residences in major cities.
According to Savills Hotels research, an increasing number of branded residence developments are being launched in partnership with international hospitality operators, including Marriott International, IHG, and Hyatt. These projects account for 60 per cent of the future development pipeline, compared with just 28 per cent of existing branded residence supply.
This shift highlights the growing influence of global operators within the sector and reflects changing development patterns, with new projects increasingly concentrated in major urban markets such as Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, and Da Nang rather than traditional resort destinations.
Alongside established hospitality developers, several local residential developers are also considering branded residences as a new approach to the premium segment. According to Mr. Mauro Gasparotti, Senior Director, Southeast Asia, at Savills Hotels, and Founder of WeHub, the global ultra-luxury residential sector is being reshaped by a larger and increasingly mobile wealth base, with the global ultra-high-net-worth individual (UHNWI) population projected to increase by 29 per cent between 2021 and 2026. At the same time, branded residences have evolved from a niche segment into a mainstream luxury product, with more than 220 new projects currently under development worldwide.
Across many of the Asia-Pacific’s major economies, rapid wealth creation is generating a larger pool of HNWIs and UHNWIs who are seeking branded residences closer to home. With global billionaire wealth having grown by 121 per cent over the past decade, demand is becoming broader and more structurally embedded within intra-Asian markets, reducing the reliance on international purchasers.
Vietnam is also on a strong UHNWI growth trajectory, reflecting the country’s expanding wealth base and rising appeal as a destination for luxury residential, branded residences, and wellness-led real estate. “The market is expected to add 40 branded residence projects to its planning and development pipeline, underscoring the sector’s growing momentum and long-term potential,” Mr. Gasparotti said.
Compared to Thailand, Vietnam’s branded residence market remains at a relatively early stage of development, but several structural factors are supporting its long-term potential. Industry experts highlight several drivers behind this outlook, including the expansion of the country’s affluent and UHNWI population, the continued recovery of international tourism, and ongoing investment in transport infrastructure.
Looking ahead, the market is expected to see a growing number of developments launched in partnership with international brands, particularly across major urban centers and established resort destinations. At the same time, pricing within the segment is increasingly reflecting the value of brand affiliation, professional management, and service standards. While branded residences in Vietnam continue to command a premium, the market is still developing its pricing benchmarks compared with more mature destinations across the region.

articles.title: Woman flashes middle finger, kicks auxiliary cop in groin while brushing teeth behind wheel in Malaysia - AsiaOne.com
articles.summary: Woman flashes middle finger, kicks auxiliary cop in groin while brushing teeth behind wheel in Malaysia  AsiaOne.comSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR — A woman who was allegedly brushing her teeth behind the wheel flashed her middle finger at an auxiliary police officer before getting out of her car and kicking him in the groin during a bizarre confrontation at Glo Damansara yesterday.
The woman then managed to escape after a struggle with the 30-year-old officer, leaving police hunting for her following the incident in Taman Tun Dr Ismail (TTDI).
According to Utusan Malaysia, the drama unfolded at about 8.38am when the officer, who was on stationary duty, spotted a Hyundai Inokom parked facing the wrong direction.
The driver was also allegedly honking at other vehicles for no apparent reason.
Brickfields district police chief ACP Hoo Chang Hook said the officer approached the car to reprimand the woman and instruct her to move her vehicle.
But instead of complying, the woman allegedly responded with an obscene gesture — all while brushing her teeth.
“However, the suspect made an obscene gesture by raising her middle finger while brushing her teeth.
“The suspect then got out of the vehicle and attempted to attack the officer before kicking him in the groin,” Hoo said, as quoted by the national daily.
The officer called for backup as he struggled with the woman and attempted to detain her, but she managed to flee before other personnel could intervene.
Police have since launched a search for the suspect.
“Efforts are actively underway to locate the suspect.
“The case is being investigated under Section 323 of the Penal Code and Section 14 of the Minor Offences Act 1955,” Hoo said.
Section 323 covers voluntarily causing hurt, while Section 14 of the Minor Offences Act concerns insulting behaviour.
Source: Malay Mail

Najib’s lawyer Shafee Abdullah reportedly said the former prime minister had received the house arrest order and terms, but was ordered not to disclose the details.
Lim said the terms of Najib’s house arrest were not an official secret and should not be kept under wraps, describing the move as “ridiculous”.
The Kepong MP said this would fuel further speculation on Najib’s house arrest, and that Malaysians deserved to know the conditions that had been set.
“Who is allowed to visit him? Can he use his phone, the internet and social media? What about watching television or other forms of entertainment and receiving guests? Is he required to wear an electronic wristband or will he be under CCTV monitoring at all times?
“Najib is still a prisoner. He is not yet a free man. This case involves public interest and may be a reference for the future implementation of house arrests.
“So the people deserve to know how imprisonment will be conducted outside of prison,” he said in a statement.
Lim urged the prisons department to make public the terms of Najib’s house arrest, saying while sensitive security-related information could be kept secret, not everything should be hidden.
“House arrest is not a holiday at a luxury bungalow. If everything is above board, why fear publicising the conditions?”
Najib was jailed in August 2022 after the Federal Court upheld his conviction of abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving RM42 million in SRC funds.
He was sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined RM210 million.
In January 2024, former king Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah exercised his pardon powers by halving Najib’s jail term and reducing his fine to RM50 million.
On Sept 18 this year, Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim granted Najib a further conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of the fine and compliance with other stipulated conditions.
Umno has set up a fund to help its former president pay the fine, with party leaders, members and supporters encouraged to contribute voluntarily.
